utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, my name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry and Mr. Huber, for the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Edina Residovic, Defence Counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. Delalic is also represented by my colleague, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Howard Morrison. I appear together with Madam Nahada Buturovic for the defendant, Mr. Mucic. My learned friend Mr. Greaves is together with me acting as consultant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. The further appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence Counsel of Mr. Hazim Delic. Mr. Delic is also defended by Tom Moran, attorney from Houston. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Cynthia McMurrey and, along with Ms. Nancy Boler, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we will start with the motion by Ms. Residovic. We will have a reply by the Prosecution, if there is any. Can we hear you, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good morning. Your Honours have before you our written submission on this matter. We ask that attachment number 3 and annexes "A" to "G" of the Prosecution's Sentencing Submission be struck from that submission and, thereby, from the record. We have two bases for making this motion, Your Honours. First, in our submission, this is a deliberate attempt by the Prosecution to place before the Tribunal documents which this Chamber and the Appeals Chamber have ruled inadmissible. I must say at the outset, Your Honour, that, in our submission, this borders on misconduct by counsel, and at least it certainly would be close to that in some national jurisdictions. In any case, in our submission, it amounts to a flagrant disrespect for the rulings and lack of deference of the rulings of this Tribunal, and it's an inappropriate attempt to circumvent decisions already handed down by two Chambers of this Tribunal. A second basis for which we say that these attachments and annexes ought to be struck is that they amount to a violation of the fair trial provisions of the Statute, Articles 20 and 21, and a violation of the Rules regarding the presentation of evidence, and those are Rules 85 and 89. By presenting to the Tribunal evidence or documents which have been ruled inadmissible, it amounts to a prejudice of detrimental effect to the accused and does not provide for a fair determination of issues before the Trial Chamber. For those two reasons, Your Honours, we respectfully request the relief sought, namely, that attachment 3 and annexes "A" to "G" be struck from the Prosecution's Sentencing Submission and from the trial record. Those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is there any other contributions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honours, on behalf of Mr. Mucic, I respectfully adopt the submissions made by Professor O'Sullivan and simply add this addendum to it, without reducing, in any way, the impact of those submissions. Although the Court is going to be seized, on many occasions, of evidence where a judicial decision has to be made to filter out those parts of any given statement which go, perhaps, to guilt and those which go to mitigation, that is never an easy exercise, even with the greatest respect to experienced Judges. Therefore, with an abundance of caution, in my submission, if there is any doubt at all as to the efficacy, effect, or direction in which any testament or statement goes, it is within the bounds of natural justice to exclude it, so that the defendant himself is certain, in his own mind, that no account, either conscious or subconscious, has been taken of that document. With that addendum, I adopt the former submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we hear Mr. Moran?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we will also join Ms. Residovic's motion, and we will join for the reasons she set forth and for two additional reasons. One, it is clear in every jurisdiction that I have ever heard of that sentencing for rules of evidence and letting evidence in is much looser than deciding whether someone is guilty or innocent. It is to provide the Court with information to sentence. But that having been said, this Court has specifically ordered that these documents not be admitted and, secondly, the Court, in its scheduling order of September 10th, said that this proceeding will be limited solely to issues relating to punishment. Those documents clearly, I believe, relate solely to guilt and innocence. I don't want to relitigate that issue. We've already done that, and I think the Court should exclude that, strike it from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like the record to reflect also that the Defence of Esad Landzo joins in the arguments of Counsel for Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we hear the Prosecution, please, in reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, the approach that's been adopted by the Defence in this case seems to proceed on the assumption that there's only one basis upon which evidence may be admissible before you. As Your Honours well know, evidence may be admissible on a number of grounds. It doesn't have to be related strictly to the issue of guilt or innocence. Mr. Moran is quite right, that when it comes to sentencing, the procedures are much different to that which apply to tendering evidence in the course of the trial in order to determine guilt and innocence. Indeed, this is reflected, if Your Honours please, by the Rules of the Tribunal, because Rule 100(A) makes reference to the fact that the Prosecutor and the Defence may submit any relevant information, which, Your Honours, is a much broader and wider term than, for example, the tendering of evidence in order to determine guilt or innocence. The material that is put before you, in our submission, specifically for the issue of the behaviour of the accused after their arrest and during the course of the trial, Your Honours, in the course of the submissions that will be urged upon you by the Defence, particularly in the annexes of Delalic, specific reference is made to the sentencing principles which apply in Yugoslavia. I'll take Your Honours to them in the course of my submissions, but you'll see by that, Your Honours, that clearly conduct after the arrest, during the course of trial, and up to the time of sentence is a matter that is appropriately considered by the Courts of Yugoslavia. They are not alone in that. There are numerous jurisdictions which permit that. It certainly comes within the rubric of relevant information, Your Honours. On that basis, that is the course taken by the Prosecution. I have a couple of cases on the point which may assist Your Honours, and there is a reference that I have to the Queen v. Albright, 1987, that's reported in 37 Canadian Criminal Cases, 3d, page 106. In that judgement, the Court is referring to an earlier decision of the Queen v. Gardener, 1982, 68 Canadian Criminal Cases, and the Supreme Court of Canada says this in relation to evidence which may be submitted during the sentencing process, as opposed to at trial. They say, and this is at page 106: "It is commonplace that the strict rules which govern at trial do not apply at a sentencing hearing and it would be undesirable to have the formalities and technicalities characteristic of the normal adversary proceeding prevail. The hearsay rule does not govern the sentencing hearing. Hearsay evidence may be accepted where found to be credible and trustworthy. The judge traditionally has a wide latitude as to the sources and types of evidence upon which to base his sentence. He must have the fullest possible information concerning the background of the accused if he is to fit the sentence to the offender rather than to the crime." There is also, Your Honours, a helpful comment in a decision, which, no doubt, Mr. Moran is familiar with, of Williams v. New York, reported at page 337, 247 United States Reports, where the Supreme Court of the United States related to a similar issue observed: "Tribunals passing on the guilt of a defendant always have been hedged in by strict evidentiary procedural limitations. But basically before and since the American colonies became a nation, courts in this country, and in England, practised a policy under which a sentencing judge could exercise wide discretion in the sources and types of evidence used to assist him in determining the kind and extent of punishment to be imposed within the limits fixed by law." They then go on and say: "Rules of evidence have been fashioned for criminal trials, which narrowly confine the trial contest to evidence that is strictly relevant to the particular offence charged. These rules rest, in part, on a necessity to prevent a time-consuming and confusing trial of collateral issues. They were designed to prevent Tribunals concerned solely with the issues of guilt of a particular offence from being influenced to convict for that offence by evidence that the defendant had habitually engaged in other misconduct. A sentencing judge, however, is not confined to the narrow issues of guilt. He is tasked with affixed statutory and constitutional limits as to determine the type and extent of punishment after the issue of guilt has been determined. Highly relevant, if not essential, to his selection of the appropriate sentence is the position of the fullest information possible about the defendant's life and characteristics. Modern concepts of individualising punishment have made it all the more necessary that a sentencing judge not be denied the opportunity to obtain pertinent information by a requirement of rigid adherence to restrictive rules of evidence properly admissible at trial." Your Honours, to suggest that, somehow or another, we are guilty of misconduct because we have put before you information which you may find of assistance when it comes at the imposition of a sentence, in light of those quotes that I have given Your Honour, is an absurd suggestion. The information that Your Honours have, you can accept or reject it. It's a matter for Your Honours. It's put there as information which we think may be of assistance to you. Because it's been ruled inadmissible in the course of the trial in no way precludes its admission at this stage if Your Honours should find it of assistance to you when you are reaching your determination on the appropriate sentence to be imposed. Those are our submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm not familiar with the decided cases of the jurisprudence on which these quotes have been cited, but I think that there is some substantive difference between a situation where mitigation of sentence is part of the proceedings before conviction, and the situation where it becomes only the proceedings after conviction. Here, it appears mitigation of sentence is part of the proceedings before conviction, and that is what our new Rules appear to suggest. It's not a differentiated procedure after conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, that the information that is put before you now and over the course of the next few days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that the theories you have put forward are wrong, because sentencing is mainly a discretionary matter, but it's the procedural rules that I'm a little worried about, because there are a few things in favour of accused persons during trial. These are not things which could be affected by the sentencing procedure, if you bring it within the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I assume that when the decision was made for Your Honours to consider sentencing matters in a more economical way, I might say, during the course of the trial, rather than after a verdict has been returned, was based primarily on the fact that it is recognised and understood that Your Honours are judicially trained, legally trained, judicial officers, who will deliberately exclude sentencing material from your consideration when it comes to the determination of guilt or innocence. I presume that Their Honours considered this when they amended the Rules to make provision for this information to be provided at this stage of the proceedings. It's interesting, Your Honours, that there's been no amendment to Rule 101, for example, which, if Their Honours were concerned about the issue that Your Honour Judge Karibi-Whyte mentions to us, they might have amended that, because, specifically, Rule 101 provides that the parties may put before the Court, in determining sentence, any aggravating circumstances. Your Honours, I would be surprised if you will hear any material or evidence of aggravating circumstances coming from that side of the room. Presumably, it's intended that the Prosecutor would put that before Your Honours, if that information is available. If that's not the case, then Rule 101(B)(i) becomes dead letter or, alternatively, there must be an opportunity, after this exercise when Your Honours return your verdict of guilty or not guilty, for the Prosecutor to then present to you evidence of aggravating circumstances. It's our understanding that that was not the intention of the Rule. The intention of the Rule was that all of these matters were to be dealt with in the course of presenting evidence at trial and that Your Honours would very carefully separate and distinguish material which is to be considered for sentence from that which is to be considered for the determination of guilt or innocence. It is on that very basis that some evidence, which is completely inadmissible for the purposes of trial, can become admissible for the purposes of sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Any documents which you have added, would they have a bearing on the quantum of sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They go to the character of the accused, which is an issue that Your Honours will be concerned with when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: To show the character of the accused, or do they relate to the guilt or innocence of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We put them up only on one basis, Your Honour, we make this very clear, it is put up on the basis of going to the character of the accused for the determination of any sentence that may be appropriate, having regard to the fact that Your Honours will want to become familiar with the circumstances of the character of the accused. That's the only basis that it is put before Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just briefly comment on this remark on the part of the Prosecution? You have already pointed to us not to seek other legislations if we have rules of our own. We have a unified proceeding here, and we have had a presentation of evidence which should be sufficient for the Trial Chamber to reach its decision. This Trial Chamber is now proceeding in the same manner as the courts in the former Yugoslavia and now in Bosnia and Herzegovina are proceeding. In other words, we have a unified proceeding in which both the aggravating and mitigating evidence may be presented in order to present all the facts of the case, but they cannot offer inadmissible evidence. This would constitute the evidence that this Tribunal has already rejected. Both this Trial Chamber and, in some cases, the Appellate Chamber has rejected some of this proposed evidence four times and six times. In our legal system, our rules of procedure also point to that, to take into account the legislations of the former Yugoslavia. First, the evidence offered by the Prosecution can be rejected on its own merits, and we stay with all the evidence which we have presented and which my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, has offered to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Morrison, have you anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Just one matter, please, Your Honours. Even on the limited basis which the Prosecution say they seek the inclusion of this evidence, that is, going after character, they make, in my respectful submission, a fundamental mistake. Before relevance and, therefore, admissibility is finally determined in respect of any piece of evidence, the Tribunal has to be satisfied as to its reliability as a fundamental pre-set of the admissibility of any evidence. It would be patently unjust to admit any document or any part of any document if there has been any doubt as to its reliability, credibility, and trustworthiness. I use the words "credibility" and "trustworthiness" deliberately, because, in his recent submission, my learned friend Mr. Niemann quoted an authority where the basis for the admission of any evidence was its credible and trustworthy nature. Now, if I may refer to you to page 3 of the submissions, this motion, as far as my learned friend madam Residovic is concerned, it says this at the centre of page 3: "Annex D contains a document which is purportedly a report on the handing over of the duties of prison warden," allegedly signed by Mr. Mucic, Mr. Delic, and Mr. Delalic. There is no proof of authenticity of this document, either in regards to its provenance or its authorship. Indeed, the Trial Chamber stated in its decision of the 19th of August, 1998: "This is a document of doubtful validity." Well, if any document is of doubtful validity, that is simply another way of saying that it is not credible. If it doesn't pass the credibility or reliability test, and that is on the criminal burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt, not on the civil test of a balance of probabilities, then it simply is inadmissible for any purpose, whether it goes as to character or as to issues of guilt. If, in any Tribunal, judges wish to find aggravating circumstances, then, of course, they are entitled to do it from credible, admissible evidence, and nothing else. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, to rather quickly explain the Supreme Court case that Mr. Niemann quoted, it's the practice in American Federal Court for a probation officer, who is an officer working for the Court, to prepare a background investigation on the defendant. It's been the practice for many years. It's changed because of our sentencing guidelines, but the Court's decision was to allow the admissibility or allow the Court to consider -- it is not even admissible evidence. It's not evidence at all. It is information that it given to the judge so that the judge can know the background of the defendant and some of the facts. Clearly, if a defendant is caught in the gaol with a weapon or is fighting with the guards or something like that, that's relevant to a sentencing decision. In fact, if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Counsel please speak up a little bit for the benefit of the interpreters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Sure. But the lack of evidence of that doesn't -- in fact, the Court can almost presume that if the Prosecutor doesn't show evidence that someone has been behaving badly in gaol, that he is behaving well. That is different from admitting or presenting to the Court, for its sentencing decision, evidence that has been excluded by a court order. For instance, again, using the American system, if a federal judge has excluded a confession because it was not taken under the proper procedures, similar to our rules where a person is warned, the Court could not consider that confession at punishment in arriving at a sentence. It's just simply not usable for anything. Here, again, no one is complaining, or at least I'm not, about evidence of my client's behaviour in custody or what he did here, what he did there. What our complaint is about is presenting to the Court documents which the Court has explicitly excluded from evidence, saying that, for whatever reason, it should not be presented to the Trial Chamber. That's a wholly different thing from evidence of showing character. Our objection is limited not to the background information, i.e., what Mr. Niemann was talking about, their behaviour, or at least my client's behaviour, between his arrest -- actually, his surrender, he wasn't arrested, he surrendered, and today, but, rather, those documents that the Prosecutor tried to get in, and the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber said, "No. We're not going to admit them."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, my colleagues have discussed, at length, the credibility of the evidence to be admitted on sentencing, but I would like to remind the Court that the Prosecution has also included, in their submission, evidence that is not relevant to the punishment of our clients, in that in their victim impact statements, they have included losses, pains, injuries, that the witnesses say themselves were a result of the war in general, the loss of their home, the loss of their income, the loss of the lives of their family. Under the Tadic decision, of course, the only relevant evidence is the evidence which is directly related to the injuries, pains, or problems associated and related directly to the defendant in this case. The victim impact statements that they have submitted as sentencing evidence and aggravating circumstances, the whole war was an aggravating circumstance, but it has to be directly related to Esad Landzo who caused that event to happen on each one of these victims. I know that, based on the Tadic decision, this Court will be able to see that 90 per cent of the victim impact statements that they presented are irrelevant to this proceeding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will take these arguments into account when the sentencing procedure will take place, because the whole thing is part of the proceedings, and we don't give a separate decision on each part of the proceedings. It is an integrated procedure. Thank you. I think the next matter we have is Ms. McMurrey's witness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm assuming that the Prosecution does not have any witnesses to present at this hearing, and the order of appearance of the Defence evidence in this sentencing hearing was reversed, and I am prepared to go forward this morning. I would like to apprise the Court that I have a change in the presentation of oral evidence. Dr. Van Leeuwen will not be appearing, and the only two witnesses we will be calling today will be Dr. Goreta and then Goran Jelisic, who is a detainee in the Detention Centre who will be present here this afternoon. So we have only two witnesses to offer oral evidence today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can proceed with your first witness now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The Defence of Esad Landzo calls Dr. Miroslav Goreta. Your Honours, while we're waiting for Dr. Goreta, I would like to offer the written statements that we are offering into evidence for mitigation to punishment for Esad Landzo at this time. They have previously been provided to the Prosecution, and I would like to submit these at this time as evidence for mitigation of punishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If I might have the assistance of the usher. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In lieu of oral testimony, the Defence would like to offer these written statements as evidence of mitigation of punishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you kindly swear the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, were those written statements admitted into evidence for sentencing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: These are your written statements?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I'm telling you, speaking for myself, I will have a look at these documents only after I have decided whether your client is guilty or not guilty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think that would be most proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The same applies to the documents which the Prosecution has added. I look at them only after I have decided whether the particular accused is guilty or not guilty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, I think that's most appropriate. I'm submitting them now just based upon the scheduling order and trying to follow the orders of this Court. So, they are submitted into evidence to be considered at your leisure, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly examine your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask the usher to move this thing? I can't see Dr. Goreta. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Goreta?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with the case, but I would like the Court to know that I have taken Dr. Goreta away from his home and family today. It is his birthday and his son's birthday. So happy birthday.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: My name is Miroslav Goreta.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Goreta, can you tell me, what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I have specialised in neurology and psychiatry, and I'm dealing with forensic psychiatry. I've been doing that for almost 30 years now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Court a little bit about your educational background, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I completed the school of medicine in Zagreb at University of Zagreb in 1969. After that I did one year internship also in Zagreb. After that I worked as a physician with the Yugoslav People's Army, which was part of my regular military service. After that, I specialised in neuro-psychiatry, that is neurology and psychiatry, at the psychiatric clinic of Vrapce where I've been working since 1971 until today. At that clinic, at that hospital, as part of my duties in 1980, after I completed postgraduate studies in psychotherapy, I defended my thesis, which had the title Psychodynamic Aspects of the Criminal Behaviour. In 1983 I defended my doctoral thesis, whose title was Psychoanalytic Approach in the Evaluation of Criminal Responsibility. As I have already told you, I've been working as a forensic psychiatrist, and as part of that I also was head of certain departments at the clinic, and I am now head of the Centre for Forensic Psychiatry. For the past four or five years I've been head of the department of the forensic psychiatry. I have organised a number of programmes for subspecialisation in the field of forensic psychiatry, which lasts three years and which is conducted for the most part at our institution at the Centre for Forensic Psychiatry. Since 1980 I've been working as assistant at the medical school of the University of Zagreb, the chair of forensic psychiatry. In the past four years I've been working as the head and organiser of these particular studies. I have four courses, I teach four courses in the field of forensic psychiatry. I have also lectured at several other postgraduate studies at the University of Zagreb, within the same field, again, forensic psychiatry. I am also a lecturer at this legal faculty at the University of Zagreb, and I teach a course entitled Forensic Psychiatry, again. I'm also president of the Croatian Association of Forensic Psychiatry, which is part of the Croatian Medical Association, and I'm on the board of the Croatian Association for Studies in suicidology. I am also a member of several other psychiatric associations and societies. As for international organisations are concerned, I would like to state that I'm a member of the International Committee for Mental Health, which has its seat in Montreal. I'm also a member of the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy, which was founded in Leuven and has its seat currently in London. I believe that this is, that I've given you the most important points as regards the question that you have asked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You were also, I see, president of the ethics committee, as far as psychiatry goes at your hospital; weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I was the president of the ethics committee at our hospital; but now I am a member of the ethics committee of the Croatian Psychiatric Association, which is an umbrella organisation for all associations that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You are widely published, you've written many articles and several books; haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Let me correct you. I'm not quite sure I understood you. Did you say ethics or ethnic committee? Of course, I was the president and a member of the ethics committee. This may be quite important in this particular context.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You are correct, I did say ethics. So, that's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court a little bit about your history as far as publications go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Don't you think you will save a lot of time if you let him give his evidence? If there is any other way you can introduce his curriculum vitae, let us do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have his curriculum vitae to introduce into evidence; unfortunately, the list that I have of publications and writings is still in Croatian. I will substitute that at a later date, but he is quite well published, and I would like to offer this into evidence at the moment, with the assistance of the usher. Just to assist, since it is in Serbo-Croatian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is evidence in mitigation of factors which are admitted in mitigation. The most important thing -- we appreciate his quality, everything is quite good; but let us hear exactly why you think there should be mitigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then I'm going to proceed on the assumption that you accept that Dr. Goreta is an expert in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Goreta, you have written one article in particular that was introduced into evidence in the Defence case as D83/4, but it was only introduced for a limited purpose. Can you tell the Court the circumstances surrounding, and the reason for the studies and the article that you wrote called Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Resulting from War Traumas and its Forensic Psychiatric Meaning?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: The basic reason for studying war trauma and its significance for forensic psychiatry was the situation that was the result of war. Our centre participated in sending a number of perpetrators of various criminal offences who participated in war activities, and for whom it was established by the Court that they were perpetrators, and they requested a number of opinions as to the forensic aspects of such disorders. So, very often we had evaluation as to the criminal responsibility, mental responsibility, the danger that a person would pose to its surroundings, and the need to conduct psychiatric therapy. In most of these cases, the Court, in view of war circumstances, emphasised the need for us to explain the extent to which the war situation could have influenced a particular individual in terms of trauma, and so on; bearing in mind, of course the situation in Croatia during the war, and also in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war, because we had a number of requests from courts in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, we were often required to throw some light on these circumstances and to discuss possible pathology of these subjects, and the evaluation, and the importance of these court evaluations. Since I worked as the head of this particular clinical department, and since I am also a lecturer and teacher, in addition to our daily practical work, that is, the drafting of our professional opinions and reports, we also tried to bear in mind, to take into account the scientific side of such expertise. This was one of the first researches that I conducted personally and which I deemed suitable for publication abroad so that necessary comparisons could be made with the other various authors from other countries, especially countries that found themselves in similar situations, that is, regional war, such as in Vietnam, the Falkland Islands, Lebanon and many other regions, which I don't need to dwell on at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Goreta, if the expert witness for the Prosecution said there was no difference in the psychodynamics of the Vietnam syndrome and the psychodynamics of the Balkan war; would he be correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: It is a matter for the international research community to accept or to refuse in the following years. I don't know. My impression, my personal impression, which I mentioned in my article, and which by no means had an objective to establish criteria, definite criteria for evaluating this, is that, as far as we are concerned, we are happy with the criteria stated in two major world psychiatric classifications. As for specific circumstances of the Balkan war, which are difficult to explain here in few words, they have been discussed in a number of papers and books by authors from the former Yugoslavia and other countries which published very precious papers on this subject. My attitude is these special circumstances can be evaluated as an additional criteria for diagnosis; and therefore, we should offer them to the international psychiatric community and also to our courts, which has been accepted now as part of our case law. As for the psychodynamics and the description of the symptom, this may not be the main purpose of this question. However, I wish to mention, as far as I'm familiar with this case, there have already been problems in regard to that; that is, the descriptive explanation of terms and symptoms, and the interpretation of these symptoms. One symptom can be, can function differently at a pharmacological level, and it can mean something completely different at this particular level, the descriptive psychodynamics. Throughout my work I have tried to integrate this descriptive pharmacological approach and the psychodynamic approach. And I thought, I hoped that such an integration, such a common approach will yield more quality results, more quality findings than a reduced approach that we had so far, which was more theoretical, and which sometimes did not pay enough attention to the subject concerned. Again, everything we say must result from our communication with the person in question, and that communication has to be put into the context of relevant classifications which are accepted today. However, this all has to be explained through the psychodynamic dimension, without which it would be practically impossible to follow the dynamics of that particular communication, the mechanisms of defence, the treatment of the victim and so on. I have to apologise for the length of my explanations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think the main question is: Can you state specifically what the main difference in the criteria is between the PTSD associated with the Vietnam war versus the PTSD and the results associated with the Balkan war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: As for the essential criteria, there are no differences, because we are obliged to accept the valid psychiatric classifications. However, I have to add that in Croatia and in the former Yugoslavia before, we were legally bound to apply criteria of the World Health Organisation, and the classification. Before the classification that was applicable, ICD-9 and DSM-3 were also valid at that time. However, in Croatia right now we are bound to apply the ICD-9 classification. There are no basic differences in these two classifications, and there should not be any. But what I offered as a possible touchstone, for practical purposes, is the fact there is a difference between a soldier going to fight in a foreign country and a soldier fighting in military operations in his own country. In many cases this was often in the vicinity of his home, where he had to defend his family, his children, his home. That particular effect further complicated his relations with his family, with his neighbours, with persons who were very close to him, but who had different political and religious convictions. In such a situation we have a very sensitive, we're dealing with a very sensitive area, and it is very difficult to define, to delineate. For example, war front, front-line, in the particular area; and one of the greatest problems that I came across throughout my work with these people is the very loosely defined role of the enemy. Enemy could be a member of the regular JNA, regular Yugoslavian People's Army, which disintegrated later on, and where there were a lot of paramilitary formations on various sides. A neighbour could also be the person who would attack the subject, that is the patient, or a neighbour could participate in informing the enemy about the subject. The neighbour could participate in a number of irregular military attacks, and so on. So, these are the specifics of the situation we are dealing with. Civilians took part in these conflicts. There were people wearing various uniforms, various types of clothes, and there were cases of Croatian army soldiers failing to recognise a fellow Croatian soldier because of a type of uniform. I'm speaking in general terms. It is quite clear we should try to evaluate the individual in every particular case, but we should also try and assess the situation and the specific area in which the events took place. My conclusions are related to the situation in Croatia in most of the cases; however, I'm very well aware of the fact that the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina was much more difficult. I can speak also as a citizen, but this can also be translated into psychiatric jargon. I wish to say that I do know that the Bosnian situation was far more complex and more difficult than the situation in Croatia. In my opinion, again, bearing in mind individual cases, all our evaluations adopted an individualistic approach, and they could be part of forensic and psychiatric expertise. This was normally accepted as expert opinion by the courts in our country.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Goreta, the article that I asked you about, the Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Results from War Trauma and its Forensic Psychiatric Meaning; that was published in a journal in the United States called Journal of Psychiatry and Law; is that a well thought of journal in international circles of forensic psychiatry?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I think that you could get a more reliable answer to that question from an American psychiatrist; however, for myself, I can say that this is one of the three most important publications, Forensic Psychiatry. We haven't mentioned the Forensic Psychiatry magazine issued by the committee that has its seat in Montreal, it's the International Journal of Mental Health and Law, and I think that this is the number one, which is immediately followed by the Journal of Psychiatry and Law, and the bulletin of the American Academy of Psychiatry and Law. I am talking about English journals, which I believe are the most interesting ones here. There is a number of other very important, very valuable journals that are published in other languages, as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher I would like to distribute and re-offer D83/4 into evidence for all purposes, before it was introduced only as something Dr. Grippon relied upon; now I believe Dr. Goreta has written it, he says it is reliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: One further question, Dr. Goreta, Judge Jan a few months ago had asked, he said since this was written in 1994, he asked whether this might still be the opinion of you in 1998. I believe this study was based on 25 people that you studied, and you've had the opportunity to study many more cases. Do your writings in 1994 still support your beliefs and opinions today?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I believe so, and if anything I am even more convinced of the correctness of the assertions which have been offered in that article. I base that on the subsequent research, one of which has been offered to the Defence counsel here, but perhaps in a form that may not rise to the level of a legal, of the highest standard, because it has not been published yet. This research continues, and this research actually encompasses 120 subjects who have been examined in the Vrapce Hospital Centre for Psychiatry, and through which these findings have actually been reconfirmed. As the head of the centre, I have worked on maybe 50 to 60 of these cases, out of 120, and have written them up; but I have also examined all the other subjects and contributed to the findings, and I believe that I have had full insight into the entire work. I want to add that the communication with those subjects, as well as the part of the subjects from this other larger study, it has been based on both the descriptive level and the psychodynamic level, which may not have been the case with some other experts, it was also not necessary, that is, the other experts who worked on the same sample. So, the cases which have been described in the first article have been more detailed, and the article that is appending is based more on the descriptive analysis and less on the, sort of the more in-depth psychological analysis, even though the majority of the psychiatrists working at our centre are aware of the fact and are able to use this method as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on the fact that Dr. Goreta has now substantiated and believes his report in 1994 is even more valid, from 25 subjects now to 120 subjects, I ask that this article be accepted into evidence for all purposes here at sentencing, in total, for sentencing purposes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What do you mean for all purposes?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I meant now you can consider that it is not just something Dr. Grippon based his opinion on. INTERPRETER: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to make it clear, the reason I'm going into this is because, if the Court, you know, taking guilt or innocence aside, chooses not to accept the affirmative defence of diminished mental responsibility, then diminished mental responsibility is still a most appropriate issue for mitigation of punishment. So, whichever way you look at it, the premise of diminished mental responsibility is appropriate for guilt or innocence and for sentencing considerations. So, now I'm just asking that this Court be allowed to read this whole article and take it as the word of this expert, in his opinion. And so, I'm offering it for sentencing purposes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In the sentencing stage we can be a little more liberal in admitting evidence, as Mr. Niemann has rightly pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The Court has to exercise its discretion, and the Court wants to make sure that no injustice is done, even in the severity of sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we certainly appreciate the discretion that is going to have to be placed upon and the burden of discretion that has to be placed upon this Court by being forced to hear sentencing evidence prior to a determination of guilt or innocence, and we have confidence that the Court is able to differentiate those evidences and the burdens they apply to. But, I guess I'm used to, when I'm offering something into evidence, I'm supposed to hear, in my jurisdiction, it's accepted or not accepted; and that's why I keep offering it. So, I'm assuming if there is no objection from the Prosecution, it is accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your main problem is you don't know how to limit your arguments. If you are proceeding in one, you know what you are offering in evidence for that purpose, and do that. That is what you are doing, you are offering Dr. Goreta's evidence for the purpose of sentencing. It's all right for the Trial Chamber to admit it for that purpose. You do not go back to areas which have been traversed and to raise the issues again, merely because you want to offer evidence for sentencing. This is what you are now trying to do. You don't go back to those areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm trying not to re-explore them and I do appreciate you pointing out that one of my main problems is maybe focusing, but I will try to concentrate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to go on to -- you have written several books dealing with the pathology of the body of people caught up in the Balkan war. Can you tell us how an intelligent, normal individual could display behaviour that is totally inconsistent with their normal pathology?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: We are talking about intelligent, normal persons. It is possible, and it has been shown, both in this war and in some other wars, that influence by some mad psychosis which is generated in such war situations, especially with characteristics which I have mentioned before as being present in a war situation in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, it is possible, and I'll say it conditionally, a normal person can be brought into a situation that his or her critical judgement becomes problematic and they reach decisions or have perceptions or experiences of reality which is completely twisted and different, based on their intelligence. I can step out of this situation in Yugoslavia and point out to the Hitler's Germany, where the top intellectuals, in one period of their lives, completely lost critical judgement with respect to the Nazi ideas and actually participated in the realisation of those ideas, and the German psychiatrists who themselves believed in the idea of Ubermensch and the pure race, and of the racial cleansing of the German people; and with full conviction, and in belief they were doing a good and even sacred thing, sent thousands of people to gas chambers. Let me take you back to the former Yugoslavia. I have to point out the influence of propaganda, the influence of the media, which are well documented, created enormous pressure on the people in those territories and created effects that were full of fear, a sense of threat, a sense of danger; and regardless of the intelligence which these people may have possessed, including intellectuals, have actually brought into question their rational judgement. It is interesting to observe such people today, after the war has ended; and when they are able to reflect on their positions and their judgements with certain distance, how a number of them cannot comprehend how at that time they were able to think in such a way and even behave in a manner that was very dangerous and which clearly could fall within the ambit of criminal acts. Some of the leading ideologues of this war were psychiatrists themselves, and I think that their names we all know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, you've dedicated a lot of your time and energy to the study of the importance of the diagnosis of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder in the assessment of criminal responsibility; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In particular, you've related the total picture of the psychodynamics of the soldier or the police officer to the commission of criminal acts during the aggression by the Serb Yugoslav JNA from 1992 to 1994; that was the focus of your study, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: What was the description of the characteristics, the basic characteristics of the group of individuals that you studied and investigated?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I do not know how wide I should go with my explanation with these characteristics, but what has been published in these articles, most subjects from these samples were young men, usually between 20 and 25 years of age, but there were also policemen, soldiers, ranging up to 40 years of age. This was logical because of the way the Croatian army was constituted, and I believe, actually, I am certain that it was a similar case in Bosnia, where there was a sudden unexpected attack which took place against these states, and the army needed to be established as soon as possible. So, the criteria of selection were very low. The basic criteria was that somebody was prepared to join in those combat operations, so, the age, social status and even the health condition was not considered that much. So, one of the answers about what conclusions we can draw from these articles, we see that a number of the subjects had already been treated by psychiatrists, and there were a number of those who already had criminal records. All this is based on the fact of this particular selection, that is, a need to organise military units as soon as possible, those units who could counter the attacks and aggression of the Yugoslav People's Army and the paramilitary units. Now, I do not want to go into any political issues over any of this, but it was the situation that this was a need to resist what was then considered as the fifth or sixth largest army in Europe. As far as their education and as far as the entire organisation, it is clear that this was far from perfect. Many of these units, at first, could not function as modern armies. Many things there were improvised, starting with the control and command to the structure and so on, but these are not psychiatric problems, strictly speaking, but it had its influence. This is what I would have to say regarding the sample. Maybe I'm going too wide here, so maybe it is better if you ask me a question that would limit it more to the psychiatric and forensic aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Basically, the group that you studied, I'm assuming, is from 20 to 25 years old, mainly with a couple younger and a few older. They were soldiers or police officers, and they were persons who, during the war, were accused of criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe that you also said that most of them had a secondary education, but that was about the limit of their education?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the basic data which are relevant, both for the first research and then the subsequent research. The individuals with higher education, college graduates, were not typical there. Mostly, these were people with elementary education or some secondary education or part thereof, and then there were also some who were peasants, that is, who came from agriculture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Would persons with a higher education behave differently? Would persons with a higher education behave differently in such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that, again, this should be done based on the individual research. If I'm to give an interpretation of the statistics here, I believe that it could be interpreted at the level of motivation. It appears that individuals with higher education were not as motivated to step into such high-risk situations as the individuals with a lower level of education were. I think it is a matter of ethics, and I would not want to go further into the analysis there. But through the research, as we came up with results, people joined in mostly for patriotic reasons or to defend their homes. As psychiatrists, obviously, we do not always just accept these simplified, straightforward reasonings, and we could easily identify other motives they had. Especially with people who had special mental disorders, these motives were correlated. It had to do with the disassociation aspects of these persons. This opened up the door to the free expression of aggression, which would even be awarded, which, as you know, is a general situation. It is not specific to Croatia. In many of these criminal acts, most of them were murder attempts, commission of bodily injury, but there were other criminal acts which were based on more material motivations, regardless of the level of rationalisation mechanisms. But overall, these criminal acts were similar to the acts which such persons had committed before the war, but now it was rationalised in order to gain a more advantageous position in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe one thing that we discussed before, in reference to Judge Jan's question, was that the factor of intelligence and a normal pathology, sometimes these people were just as affected with their intellectual ability to function and reason normally during this war situation as someone who was not as intelligent. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Of course. I also believe that in the layperson's -- even in court, the intelligence or IQ can be used as a criterion for this person's ability to distinguish between good and bad and that this is sufficient to judge the criminal behaviour. But I must say that this is a big illusion. It is true that such persons in an experimental situation, they may score well in a psychological test, but in some other real-life situation, especially in a situation which has strong effects linked to them, such as anger or fear or a sense of threat, their rational behaviour can be reduced and, in some extreme cases, can even be excluded. Now, I'm talking here about the very intensive effects, and I do not need to point out their presence in this general chaos and the sense of threat which was present during the war in Croatia and Bosnia. However, we have additional factors which may further complicate the situation which is a very frequent situation of alcoholic intoxication. I know that in certain legislation, it is not allowed, especially for psychiatric analysis, but a Court can evaluate a state of tensions, but there are some pathological states of tension which the normal action, I believe, falls within the ambit of psychiatric evaluation, and it will be evaluated as such by the Court. The third factor may be drugs which, in a wartime situation, are usually not controlled and were largely available for consumption. The use of such drugs can also contribute to the reduction of, let's say, an expected functioning, which is out of proportion with the intellectual potential of a particular individual, so that such an individual, in a particular real-life situation, may behave completely differently from what they would have normally done, especially in a time of war where they are, let's say, even a leader of a unit, and then he places both his and his soldiers' lives in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please inform the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McMurrey, I thought you have done enough on the general background now. This is a mitigation proceeding, and I think you should focus on Mr. Landzo's mitigation evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to try to stick exactly with my specific questions that I had, which were focused from the beginning, but somehow we have gotten off track. I will do my best. Thank you. If I may proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Goreta, you have written extensively on the application of PTSD on criminal responsibility. It is your opinion that PTSD alone will not excuse criminal responsibility of the individual, but PTSD, combined with the total psychodynamic pathology of the individual, can and often does rise to the level of diminished responsibility. I think what you're saying is that you have to take in the whole, total individual. Would you explain that just a bit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I do not exclude the possibility for the PTSD to be the reason for a complete exclusion of criminal responsibility. In our criminal law, we use the term "mental responsibility," "mental accountability," and so on. We have to bear in mind that there are several editions of our criminal texts. The term we use is "mental responsibility." We have to take into account flashback situations, for example, hallucinations. These are the phenomena which, at the level of the individual, may be identical to an event that the individual experienced during the war, and now these phenomena are reappearing, resurfacing in the real-life situation when there is something similar that causes it. The situation may be completely different. The individual may find himself with his friends, family, and so on. If, in such a situation, an individual commits a criminal offence and his behaviour is psychopathological, then that person can be deemed mentally irresponsible. If the Court accepts such an explanation, that person can be held criminally accountable. We've had such examples in relevant literature, but I haven't come across any of that during my work. The most frequent situation we've dealt with is the PTSD being influential in the sense that it decreases, diminishes, the mental responsibility. We had a different system of various levels of criminal mental responsibility. We've had severely diminished mental responsibility and so on. It is possible, once again, that such a phenomena can occur at the level of PTSD. However, it is more likely that we are dealing with a combination of various influences, that is, primary disorders, personality disorders, as they are described in one of the classifications that I have mentioned some time ago. Then we have stressful reactions, reactive states, and so on. As far as the American classification is concerned, there was no diagnosis of this acute stress disorder, which has now subsequently been introduced, and there are reasons for its introduction. It is something that is quite important, but at the time when we were doing our analysis, we often gave a diagnosis which did not exist according to the American classification. Had we done that recently, we would have used the American type of classification. The reason I am mentioning this is the fact that PTSD is something that is defined as a disorder which lasts up to a month. If, however, it continues outside that period of time, then it will get a slightly different diagnosis. Therefore, you can see that a purely theoretical application of a diagnosis, without properly taking into account other factors, is not something that is objective, because we are also dealing with the various conventions, various descriptions, of particular illnesses. Therefore, you can have various results, various findings, in different analyses. Also, I would like to mention, once again, the importance of the impact of alcohol and other types of intoxication. Those were the most common combinations that led to a potential mitigation of criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe what you're saying is that PTSD, in severe cases, can rise to diminished mental responsibility, but most often, when you have found that there was diminished mental responsibility, it was due to a combination of either a personality disorder with PTSD or some kind of addictive alcohol or drug addiction combined with PTSD; would that be fairly accurate?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: This would be accurate. However, I have to state, once again, that the diagnosis is only the first element for our evaluation. The subject who receives a particular evaluation is then viewed within the context of the criminal offence with which he has been charged. Therefore, a person who commits, intentionally, a theft or forgery of a document or something similar, regardless of the severity of his PTSD, he can be fully mentally responsible. However, if such an individual is acting in a situation which is particularly difficult for him in terms of his effective functions, then we, as psychiatrists, can evaluate him as not being fully mentally responsible. This can lead to a mitigation of sentence. Again, we have to bear in mind the individual, and we have to bear in mind all of the factors that influence the individual and all of the factors that influence the behaviour of the individual at the relevant times, at the time of the commission of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you talk about these effective functions, I believe that the key that you're looking at is whether he's able to understand his actions and to control his actions at the time that he committed the crime. Would that be the key that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: We always evaluate both intellectual and willing functions, volitional functions. These can be equally reduced in a particular situation. In extreme cases, these volitional functions may even be excluded. In some cases, however, there may be a different problem. There may be a person who understands his behaviour. There may be a person who is fully aware of the fact that he is about to commit a criminal offence. However, that person may be in such an effective situation that he is acting out of fear, a sense of threat or danger, and he, therefore, cannot fully use that awareness. Because of that, a crime is committed. In view of all of these factors, we can, therefore, talk about mitigating circumstances. This is, I believe, defined in a similar way in most of the legislations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In your studies that you conducted on these soldiers and young police officers, can you tell the Court what the general victimology was? Who were the victims that they chose?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I believe that there are two large groups of victims. There is a group of victims who were injured parties in the combat area, in the area of military operations. In our analysis, we had the so-called suspicious Serbs, that is, the persons who, in spite of their awareness of their own involvement in potentially criminal acts, those were the persons who were thought to be collaborators or informants of enemy forces or were thought to hide weapons, to inform the other side of specifics of grid references, and so on, that is, the persons who were thought to be somehow involved in military activities. In the psyche of these persons, there is something on the basis of which they were treated as members of paramilitary forces. However, there were those who participated in real military actions, and these persons were, in most cases, victims. Very often, they were taken prisoner, were detainees who were not detained in any regular prison facilities. They were detained, for example, in schools or some other makeshift locations. These situations are very harsh for such individuals and can, somehow, be related to the post-traumatic stress disorder. These persons were victims of such perpetrators. These are the areas closest to battle zones. However, in the area where there were no military operations, such as Zagreb, where soldiers would come for rest and recuperation, very often, the victims were civilians, Croats or members of some other nationality that was not the enemy nationality. However, because of the conflict, these persons were somehow directly or indirectly related to the military situation. These persons may have been told that they were not very good soldiers, that they were not participating in a proper way in the war, that they had some kind of connections with the enemy, and so on. Very often, we were dealing with persons who had a narcissistic problem, and then they reacted out of anger and, very often, again, they were in an inebriated and intoxicated state, and they would pick up victims among the citizens of the Croatian nationality. Let me give you an extreme situation, an extreme case: There is the idea of an enemy which is highly paranoical. Many Hungarians or Italians, for example, were victims, people who were members of some neutral nationality, neutral ethnic background, because these perpetrators thought, believed, that they were Serbs who were somehow colluding with the enemy and who were about to attack them in the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In your study of the soldiers who committed crime during this time, you came up with some general consistencies in their situations. I believe one of them was the heightened feeling of being endangered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that I mentioned this during my introduction, and I have offered several examples. This is accurate. However, there is something that was a realistic danger at the time. I'm sure you've come across a number of examples of that. People had a permanent sense of being endangered, and one could never know when such feelings could result in very severe situations. You have the example of Sarajevo, for example, where parts of the town could be shelled at any time from the surrounding hills. All citizens of the town of Sarajevo at that time had a long-lasting feeling that they could become victims any time of the day. We had similar situations in Vukovar or Dubrovnik. This was a realistic type of danger. This was something real. However, in addition to that, there was also the problem of rumours, if one can call them that, and the media propaganda. All these mechanisms that I have mentioned are here at play. We have situations where people react aggressively, paranoid, towards all members of the so-called enemy nationality, enemy religion, or enemy political party. This can be related to any such segment of the social life. Any person who had any kind of association with these, this person can be viewed automatically as an enemy, as a suspicious person, who would do something against the perpetrator in the future. This is very important in terms of social psychology. This, by all means, intensifies the feeling of being in danger. We all know that there were lots of cases of neighbours killing neighbours, members of one family killing members of the other family, and so on. In the Croatian army, for example, you could have an Albanian soldier or a Serb soldier, and his need to demonstrate his loyalty to the Croatian army was far greater than the need of simple soldiers. He felt compelled to act braver and so on. He could have felt the need to show himself off. All these mechanisms should be taken into account and related to the individual situation, of course, bearing in mind the general psycho-pathological context of the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The second consistent factor that you found in them was the undefined enemy, which we've already talked about. I believe the third consistent factor that you found in them was this breakdown of the law-based state and their need to punish the offenders. Can you just tell us a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Again, I do not wish to be subjective. I think it's common knowledge that neutral institutions, neutral scientists, neutral scholars, have pointed out that particular problem, that is, that in many areas that were affected by the war, there was a breakdown of the law-based state. Of course, even today, we have similar problems. There was a total disintegration of the legal system almost everywhere in the former Yugoslavia, and the society itself could not function properly. This goes also for the military. One could see that the hierarchy, the organisation, the structure, did not really function. Many units were acting only according to the orders of the low-level commander and had no contact with higher authority. People had the feeling that they were defenceless, that there was nobody they could complain to, that there was nobody they could sue. They had to interact with their fellow unit members and so on. When they found themselves in the situation where they were able to capture the enemy or send him to prison, these people, these individuals, experienced it as something very, very unusual, something that was not likely to happen, and so forth, because they had heard of many prisoner exchanges. There were quite a few people there, quite a few prisoners, who were thought to be war criminals, and these individuals had their own sense of justice. It is, at this point, that their superego comes into play. This is this fear where all social laws are irrelevant. These individuals thought that they could take justice into their own hands and that they could act as judges to people whom they deem to be war criminals. They thought that they were doing a good thing. They thought that they were doing a favour to their state, which could not properly function at the time and which could not organise proper legal proceedings. Again, we have to take into account all other psychological mechanisms, and we can also bear in mind our common idea, our common view, that every crime should be punished. But I better, perhaps, stop here, because we are entering a rather complex area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, the fourth consistency you found among your subjects was a transference of aggression. Can you explain that to the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: It is a well-known mechanism, when we are unable to counter the aggression because of the circumstances, that then we will easily and quickly transfer this aggression to someone else who does not have this dimension of threat to us, or where we can express this aggression without severe circumstances. Again, in relation to PTSD, if a soldier would be exposed to a high-stress situation, such as death or mutilation of some of his fellow soldiers or members of his family or destruction of property, and when he was not able to return this aggression, then you have a mechanism which would be a short-circuited affect, where this aggression is transferred to someone else who is, in any way, connected or associated with his perception of the enemy. In precisely such a case where you had killings of prisoners, killings of neighbours, or infliction of severe bodily injury to such persons, this would be the mechanism of transference of aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Goreta, you have read the previous reports of the other mental health experts. You have read the indictment, and you have reviewed most of the documents in this case. Do you remember a specific incident, including the testimony of Mr. Landzo before this Court, a specific incident with an older man named Bosko Samoukovic at Celebici. Can you relate this to this concept of transference of aggression, so that the Court can understand. This is a prime example, in your opinion, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: On the basis of information which you have just mentioned which I learned, I believe that this case would fit very well into the interpretation which we have just given.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Was there a brutal act that Mr. Landzo had viewed out at Repovci? And then upon return to the Celebici camp, did he exhibit the transference of aggression when he arrived back at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I know, both from the Court transcript and from the reports of other psychiatrists, and obviously from my conversation with Mr. Landzo, that what preceded this was his knowledge of the death of nine compatriots of his, among whom were some people who were close to him. I believe that he may have even seen some of the mutilated bodies. This is information which I gained from Mr. Landzo, so this could be brought under the umbrella of the PTSD. It must have been an exceedingly traumatic experience with respect to somebody who was close to him, so this could have been a reason for this type of reaction. We, again, go back to this case. If this was experienced for the first time, it would be an acute stress disorder, but if it was a repeated experience, which was the case with people who spent a prolonged time at the battlefront, then these traumas would multiply and reactions would be enhanced, and they would then compromise the psychic functioning even more. With respect to Mr. Landzo, there are some earlier stress situations or other traumatic situations I mentioned, especially his confrontation with the brutal killings in a camp, which allegedly was run by HOS, one of the Croatian military formations in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, the fifth consistency that you found in many of your subjects was centred around the special relationship between the commander and the offender. Can you explain a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes, I can, and I believe that this is very important too. I would, again, like to stress the significance of a situation where life, in a zone where all ties with a law-based state has been severed, and his commander -- let me use a hyperbole here: His commander would be his god. This is where the soldier transfers his superego first, because the commander knows what good or what evil is. Let me refer you, again, to the situation where they thought that the enemy was going to destroy their heritage, their families, their properties, everything. So this significance would be enhanced in comparison to a regular army situation. That meant that any order is carried out without any critical judgement, and I'm referring to my own personal experience here. I spoke to a number of perpetrators. It is not that they carried out the orders. They needed, almost, to guess what the commander would like them to do but may not be able to tell them because of all kinds of political and other circumstances under which the war was waged at the time. The commander is somebody to whom all this ethical system, so to speak, is transferred. Also, his sense of responsibility is transferred, because if the commander ordered something, "He knows better, and I need to carry this out." The model that I'm offering here should not be applied indiscriminately to any case. When it came to expertise, some of these soldiers, when analysed, would say that they were betrayed by their commanders. When these commanders would then be brought to testify, they said that they never ordered any such thing, and then, at the subjective level, this would be experienced as betrayal. It becomes a catastrophe, because the communication between the soldier and their commander was such that it is a great betrayal, and it generates a depressive reaction. There were even cases when this happened in a wartime situation. They were even attacking and, in some cases, even killing their commanders because of this sense of disappointment and betrayal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: This heightened importance and significance of the superior is worsened in a closed sphere such as the Celebici camp, wouldn't it be?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I cannot specifically speak of Celebici, but I can give you the generally known information regarding concentration camps or similar types of camps which are totalitarian institutions and where control is complete on the part of the people who run them. Obviously, it was manifested in its worst aspect against the prisoners, and if there was any disobedience of orders, this could also be turned against the person who did not carry out the order.
