These mechanisms in the camps such as you mentioned were obviously there, and surrendering your own integrity into the hands of the leader or whoever was issuing orders there, that was never a matter for discussion. It was an extreme situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The sixth factor that you found consistent with these people who did commit crimes during wartime was the accessibility to arms which wasn't there before the conflict; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes. That was a very serious problem. It is a problem that continues to be present in the regions which have nothing to do with the wartime situation anymore. Let me give you an example. You have quarrels, let's say, in bars and restaurants about, let's say, an unpaid bill or something which used to result in fist fights. Now you have weapons and even hand grenades used in such situations. When the former JNA barracks were taken over, there were huge amounts of weapons which ended up in the hands of civilians, and they still have not been retrieved to date. Psychologically speaking, what is important here is that if a person has problems with his or her aggression or narcissism and similar things, weapons serve those persons to overcome such deficiencies, something which they lack, which is a lack of a sense of power, of control. This is why such persons are additionally motivated to acquire such weapons or to join such formations where, by use of such weapons, they could demonstrate their power or strength. This is a universal phenomena, and we very frequently encountered it with people who were otherwise insecure, fearful, or had other identity disorders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, can you just tell the Court what materials you did review before you met with Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Before I met with Mr. Landzo, I reviewed materials from the Court proceedings here, which I believe you may be better able to advise the Trial Chamber as to the dates. I believe this refers to July. It could have been later too. I also reviewed materials where the written expert reports by expert psychiatrists and psychologists were enclosed. However, I did not have enough time to review such voluminous material, but I was able to read through it once over, and if I'm asked to, I probably can comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When, you reviewed the opinions of the other experts, did you think that their evaluations were fairly thorough in total? Not individually, but in total, was it a fair evaluation of Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I believe that I am not in a situation where I can really give you a very qualified opinion on the extent of these reports. I have only spent the last ten days reading them. I spoke to Mr. Landzo for three and a half hours only, whereas, other experts had had an opportunity to talk to him much longer. In giving my opinion, I must first say that I have not done everything I usually do in conducting a full-scale expertise, but as far as I can tell, this was not what was asked of me. I was just invited here to give some views on the forensic aspects relating to the wartime traumas. With respect to everyone else who has worked on the expert reports and opinions here, I would say that they were of varying degrees, but what all the experts seem to be saying is that they all agreed that this was not a case of any kind of mental disease or illness that was involved here. Also, there were no mental disorders caused by any organic or chemical causes, even though there were some indications that, during one period of time, he may have consumed larger amounts of alcohol, that is, at one time, which, from my experience, was very frequently the case during that period of time, but it was not critical enough to rise to the level of addiction. Also, everybody agreed that Mr. Landzo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Doesn't that take the case out of the British Homicide Act?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to follow-up. I believe he was talking about an organic problem. I don't believe that he mentions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He talks about the normality of --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, mental disease --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- mental development or disease origin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, I think there is mental disease and mental illness, and then there's organic problems which come from a birth defect or something like that. I believe that maybe he's confused, and I will clear that up in a few moments, because I believe mental disease and mental illness would fit under the category of personality disorder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly would object to Ms. McMurrey testifying about the witness being confused. I believe the witness's testimony is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We will leave that to the witness, won't we?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I will clear it up, but I would also like to remind the Court that this is in sentencing only, not to be considered in the guilt or innocence phase of this trial. So as the evidence stands for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The diminished ability has two dimensions. Firstly, relating to guilt, it reduces the degree of homicide, murder to manslaughter. Second, a sentence reducing the quantum sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Of course, I really will clear this up with a follow-up question. As a matter of fact, I was going to go ahead and introduce his report into evidence first, and then I will follow-up, if the Court would so like, but I will ask him right now, because this is very important.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You said, upon review of the other experts' evaluations, that you saw that they did not find any mental disease or illness, but in your expertise as a forensic psychiatrist, personality disorder, combined with a PTSD, would be a mental illness or disease, just not an organic mental illness; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I would object to the leading nature of these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just thought I would expedite the answers to this by -- I am asking a leading question, and I ask that maybe I be allowed to ask that leading question in this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm sure it's too technical for you, who is a layperson, to ask him such questions. He tells you what it is, not you telling him what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm just asking him to clarify his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are not qualified to give evidence like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't know that I'm so much a layperson after all I've read recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are not qualified to give evidence like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm just teasing, but I would like to ask him if that is his opinion or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has his opinion to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He's an expert witness. He's not a witness as to fact. So the question of leading questions really does not rise here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He knows what he says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is a fact that you can certainly ask. You know the question, suggesting the answer itself --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Normally, I would agree with Your Honours, and, in fact, we have not objected, given a very large amount of leading questions, but in this particular case, given the circumstances, we do believe it's objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him answer the question. He deserves the right to answer whatever questions are put to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Should I repeat it, Dr. Goreta, or do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: It's not necessary. Thank you. I only feel the need to say that a discussion on what is a disease and what is a disorder were very detailed. I can reopen this discussion, but I'm not sure how much use we will have of that. In short, a disease is something that is defined, and let me give you an example. Let's say schizophrenia, a manic depressive psychosis, paranoid psychosis, or an alcohol-induced delirium, in other words, severe damage of psychic functions with a severance from reality, but what we're trying to talk about today is part of disorders. These are mental disorders. Specifically, we are actually talking about personality disorders. A moment ago, I said that all the diagnoses, which were not accepted by the previous experts, and what I have just started saying, what was accepted by most of them, is that Mr. Landzo has a combination of personality disorder from the category which I mentioned and based on both the classifications that are in use. The question is only which of these personality disorders is dominant, given that what was mentioned was the dependent personality disorder and the schizoid personality disorders, the disassociative personality disorders, and maybe one or two others. The analysis of the entire material, and my clinical impression from this single, but still long enough, conversation seems to support the findings which go to the dependent personality disorder. However, I, too, agree that this is a combination of several personality disorders, which is why, in this short report, I specially mentioned his problem of uncertain identity, which, in the classification, may be found in different places, and I may have omitted to say this. I think that this is exceptionally important with a narcissistic personality disorder and a borderline and schizoid personality disorders. That means, in all cases, a problem of identity. This has been analysed in great detail in a number of expert findings. To use a situation of the false self, which is not so well-known, when the subject does not have a well-defined personality and tends to partially take over identity of some other persons and is always seeking objects with whom he may identify and whose models of behaviour they will absorb, that's another aspect. The third aspect is the problem of narcissism, which, again, may not be related to a single disorder. It is present with four or five different categories, the most present with the narcissistic, but also with paranoid, with borderline, and with disassociative personality disorders. I'm leaning towards the opinion that this dependent personality disorder is in the foreground and that the other aspects complete the diagnosis, and they may account for his biography during the war and also his biography overall. Another thing that I want to mention here is the post-traumatic stress disorder. Again, from today's point of view, if I were to analyse all these conditions, I think that it would be very difficult, because six or seven years have gone by. Looking at the entire material and the opinions of all the experts, we see certain differences in opinion as to when this PTSD actually has set in, in his case, what intensity did the symptoms have, what forensic relevance they may have, and how reliable the information on these extreme traumatic situations are, that is, the situations which we presume may have caused this disorder. I am inclined to accept that this disorder did exist, whereas, in Mr. Landzo's case, a number of arguments were offered for this theory. In addition to the psychiatric criteria, there were also psychological tests offered too. I apologise. Is everything clear now? I probably pushed some button.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Goreta, we still have one question left to be answered. I believe, in summary, what you have just said is, yes, in your opinion, he had a personality disorder with dependent personality in the forefront, and then you list several others that he exhibited also, combined with PTSD. In your opinion, do these rise to the level of a mental illness under the definitions that we're dealing with or an abnormality of the mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't see the relevance of this. I don't see the relevance at all. If you're asking him any causes for mitigation, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he's a forensic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please, I have told you what you should do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You wrote a report based on your meeting with Mr. Landzo. With the assistance of the usher, I would like to -- you wrote this report this past Friday, October 9th, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You believe that report accurately reflects your opinions, based on the time that you had to spend with Mr. Landzo and the material that you have reviewed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies. When I interrupted myself, I thought that my communication here was interrupted. I did not say that this was my opinion of the PTSD. My opinion is that there are no current clinical symptoms, which does not mean that it may not reoccur if the retraumatisation took place, in other words, the manifestation of another trauma which may mobilise, again, such symptoms. This is just what I wanted to say in closing. Let me move on to the next point. I don't know about the terms, if it is "disease" or "illness" that is being used, and, again, let me repeat, Mr. Landzo does not have a mental disease, but he has a serious psychological disorder, which I think we called a personality disorder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know whether Ms. McMurrey briefed you on the need for your giving evidence in these proceedings. All evidence about his mental condition, about his mental state, has been given in the proceedings proper. In these particular proceedings, you are merely invited to give evidence relating to mitigation. We are not reopening all matters about his mental condition or anything which concerns that. So I don't think we should go back into those proceedings and allow this. We have done enough of that for the whole morning, and it appears that you are continuing with the matter, and I don't think it is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want it known, for the record, that diminished mental responsibility is the issue for sentencing also. Therefore, even though what is evidence as far as guilt and innocence goes has been given, and the Court has that body of evidence, this body of evidence is still relevant to sentencing. So his mental capacity, his mental responsibility, is relevant at this point for sentencing purposes also. In this phase, it's only mitigation of punishment. In that phase, it's a special defence, but it's still relevant to both phases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think you understood what I said. We are not reopening whatever we have done before now. This is what I've just said. I thought it's simple enough for a normal, average person to understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Goreta, you have written this report, and that report reflects your opinions on Mr. Landzo's mental state at the moment, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, you met with Mr. Landzo on Thursday of this week, October 8th, the day you arrived here, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: How was your meeting with Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: My meeting with Mr. Landzo was a three and a half hour conversation on all relevant circumstances of which I was aware and which I needed to address here as my own and as I just understand are the focus here. It was based on everything that I had read before, and as I assumed it was going to be just one conversation, I focused on all the aspects that may confirm or go counter to the conclusions already present there. Mr. Landzo, as I pointed out, was very open, very motivated for cooperation, so that he was able to provide valuable information about the situation. Now, a certain situation he was not able to fully reconstruct, and he justified that by a certain amount of loss of memory, but otherwise, he answered everything that I asked of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to go back to Dr. Van Leeuwen's report or his testimony where he mentioned this concept of vulnerability. Can you explain where that fits into the diagnosis of his personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: There have been several questions in relation to this particular issue. I can say that this falls, within this response, to that part of the personality which I referred to as narcissistic personality disorder. It is a common characteristic for all narcissistic personality disorders, whether within the diagnosis of the narcissistic personality disorder itself, or within some other area, where these problems are particularly emphasised. These are very sensitive problems. If anything can trigger their sense of self-respect, and it is in this area where certain bad or dark characteristics of these personalities are being disclosed. It is in these type of situations that these individuals can overreact. This can seem, to a neutral observer, as something very exaggerated or unnatural. However, for the person who has suffered such a disorder, who has experienced this type of aggression, this, itself, can lead to very aggressive reactions, which are often defined as a narcissistic anger.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: By the way, Dr. Goreta, Mr. Landzo doesn't display the characteristics of a sadistic personality, does he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: A diagnosis of a sadistic personality as a separate psychiatric entity simply does not exist, although there has been an idea to incorporate it within the DSM-IV classification. What I can say in respect of Mr. Landzo, regardless of the formal existence of the definition of this type of disorder, is that what can be termed as a sadistic disorder was not found by myself during the conversation with Mr. Landzo. This is something that I could not, was not able to recognise as an important factor in any of the reports who, in the past, examined Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Also, Dr. Goreta, you didn't see that Mr. Landzo displayed any anti-social or dissocial behaviours either, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: It is very clear that Mr. Landzo, as part of his behaviour, which is incorporated in the indictment, did exhibit certain aggressive reactions. However, these aggressive reactions, if viewed in the context of his life and his behaviour in general, are simply not sufficient to justify the diagnosis of the dissocial personality disorder, because the fundamental criterion for that type of disorder, is the existence of a lasting model of dissocial behaviour. Mr. Landzo may have had isolated aggressive acts which were related to a certain conflict situations in his life which were not part of his stay in the camp. Or his aggressive reactions may have been related to the general situation in the camp at the time, and this is something I have already discussed, the type of communication in the camp and so on. So this may have something to do with the structure of Mr. Landzo's personality. This is the specific personality structure which is responsible for some possible reduction of his ability to control, to have control over his own acts and to comprehend the full significance of his acts. There is another argument which goes against the theory of dissocial personality disorder in the case of Mr. Landzo. In a prison context, these individuals would retain the same type of behaviour. They would enter into conflicts with guards and other detainees, and they are inclined to suicidal actions, taking large quantities of pills and so on. So this same pattern of behaviour would still take place in the prison situation. This is something that I could not find. This is something that I could not conclude on the basis of my conversation with Mr. Landzo and on the basis of the previous reports. He had adapted well to the circumstances of the prison life. He felt the need to respond to the requirements of the prison environment that he was in at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: By the way, dissocial is for ICD-X, is that the same thing as the anti-social personality disorder under DSM-IV?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. There are certain discussions as to the right term for this particular disorder, but, in general, I can agree with that. There have been other diagnosis as well, and this was all discussed in the context of pathological social personality disorders. However, this term, psychopathological, has been left out, because it affects the communication with the patient at the hospital and at the court, but these are identical categories.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I notice it's ten after one. I have about thirty minutes more worth of questions, so I would like to know if we would break now or if you would like me to continue. I have a couple of more pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have the whole day for your questions. We will have to break now and come back after lunch. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.11 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we're waiting for the witness, I have another written statement that was just given to me by Mr. McFaden from the U.N. Detention Centre, which I would like to offer into evidence as a written statement in support of mitigation for sentencing, if the Court would allow me to do so now? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Here's the original and there's the copies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed with your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Goreta, in your review of all the materials, you came across testimony that described the behaviour of Esad Landzo during his stay in Celebici camp and his behaviour when he was assigned to the duties at Musala Prison. How do you explain the differences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have no translation. I understand, but it is better that I have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you for telling us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'll ask it again, yes. In your review of all the materials, you came across testimony that described the behaviour of Esad Landzo during his stay at the Celebici camp and his behaviour while he was assigned to his duties at Musala Prison. How do you explain the difference?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: If we assume that the diagnoses are accurate and the situations in both camps are properly described, then this kind of change would further justify the diagnosis that's been offered, in view of the emphasised need of the accused to adapt himself to the circumstances and to the persons he depends on, including, of course, his superiors or a person that he identifies with and has high esteem for. In other words, he's the kind of person who would try to adapt himself as much as possible as to fulfil the expectations of these persons who I have just mentioned. So if the organisation and the system, the atmosphere, in these two camps was different, this would be another explanation for the change in his behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Through your review of the materials and also through your conversation with Mr. Landzo, you are aware of the different treatments and therapies that he has received in the last couple of years. Can you tell the Court what therapy he has undergone and what kind of provisions have been made to try to heal him of those problems?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I do not have a full insight into all of the therapies that have been conducted with Mr. Landzo, because the therapists have not provided a full description for the needs of the Court, which, from the ethical point of view, is fully justifiable. So I do not know exactly how the treatment went. However, I can surmise that a certain psychotherapy has been conducted, and that psychotherapy probably did not go into any deep assessment, evaluation, any deep analysis that would disclose all kinds of problems. What has been conducted was a so-called superficial psychological analysis. In addition to that, the accused has probably been treated with certain medicine which had to help him overcome his depressive state. The therapy that has been conducted or the therapies, we cannot expect such therapies to restructure his personality fully, because, as it has already been mentioned in the diagnosis, we are dealing here with states and disorders which are long-lasting and which probably have causes in his childhood. These diagnoses can only be established after the age of 18. Therefore, we cannot expect him to change completely. We cannot expect his personality to alter completely. However, and I believe that this has been achieved, his characteristics, through therapy, which would make him more insightful as to his behaviour so far, this therapy has achieved a certain objective. In the future, it can be, therefore, expected that he would be feeling much better and that he would be more self-assured and self-confidant. The final result would have to be his lesser dependence on authorities and persons he tends to identify with. For the patient, the accused, to accept a normal type of existence without any violations of law, I think that this is possible, and I believe that this adaptation can be achieved. Again, I do not know what the outcome of these proceedings will be. When the accused is finally free, and once he finds himself in a situation in which he will not experience these risks, I think that things will be much better. Therefore, this is why I stated in my report that this environment should not be his former country, in his home, and that he should not return to Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is, therefore, to be expected that he will be able to function normally in a different kind of environment. As for the dependent personality disorder or the characteristics thereof, which were rather risky in a certain environment, could, in a positive kind of environment, be factors of a better adaptability. Because if he finds himself in a situation where he would have a mature authority to follow, to be guided by, a person who would influence him in a positive way, I believe that he will be perfectly able to function without any major problems. If there had not been war in that country, just as many other people, he would not have been the subject of these psychotherapies. These people cannot be judged as cases of mental illness, but because of the circumstances, they acted the way they did, and they ended up needing psychotherapy and some kind of medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In summary, I believe that you support the general diagnosis of the other mental health experts that have been here, in that there was a basic personality disorder, that had he not experienced the trauma that he did, he probably could have lived a normal life; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You asked this question earlier on today, whether he confirmed the opinions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You asked him earlier in the morning whether he confirmed the opinions of the other psychiatrists and psychologists. He gave his answer. Why do you want to repeat this question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. If the Court is satisfied, I will go on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your basic diagnosis is still PTSD plus -- I mean, a basic personality disorder, plus a PTSD that occurred in 1991 or 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But in addition to that, I stated that the symptomatology that is currently applicable today does not have any influence on that, because I do not see any reason to question the accuracy and the objectivity of the diagnosis which has been offered by high-level psychiatrists.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your general prognosis about his future is stated in your report that you have written, but can you just tell us how you feel about whether he is rehabilitated or his rehabilitation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I believe that this is possible, and I believe that I have already answered that question in some detail. However, there are certain criteria which should be met in order to avoid a possible reoccurrence of such a situation. One of the preconditions would be for the accused to continue his life in a different environment, an environment that would be an incentive as to a full resocialisation, and other factors of risk should be avoided. I don't know what will happen with him, but in any other legal system, if he should continue his life in prison, I suggest that he no longer continues the current therapy. I believe that this therapy has already yielded very good results. I think that all modern principles of criminology should be respected and that once he's free, it should be ensured that he is still under some kind of professional surveillance, in the sense that he should be, somehow, guided by experts in that area, social workers, psychologists, and so on. If all these criteria are met, I really believe that it would be possible for him to rehabilitate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, you are aware that Mr. Landzo did attempt to commit suicide on previous occasions. How does that relate to an anti-social or dissocial personality disorder, which you have said that Mr. Landzo does not have?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: The suicide attempt is a non-characteristic type of reaction which, however, can be found in various types of classifications. Even normal, conditionally speaking, people, when they find themselves in crisis, can attempt a suicide. So that particular symptom, that kind of behaviour, can, by no means, be a decisive criteria for offering any diagnosis. When I spoke about anti-social personality disorder, I emphasised the permanent need of such people to act aggressively towards their environment which, sometimes, can have elements of criminal behaviour. As suicidal reactions with anti-social types are a symptom of this suppressed aggression, often it takes place when they cannot express that aggression. At that particular moment, they express aggression towards themselves, but this is not characteristic. Whether a person is going to cut his or her veins or inflict pain on himself or herself or use any other forms of self-punishment, this is a different area. This, by itself, is not sufficient for a diagnosis of an anti-social or dissocial personality disorder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, isn't suicide a symptom or a reaction for other personality disorders also?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Again, it is not characteristic. It can be found with various types of personality disorders. Very often, they are a consequence of a depression, but we can also have them with some other cases. For example, while discussing a PTSD, in Croatia, for the past several years, we have seen an increase in suicide attempts with the persons who have that particular diagnosis, that is, PTSD. Again, I do not want to claim that the only reason for their suicidal behaviour is the PTSD. However, it is certain that this is more frequent with these types of persons. Another important aspect is the fact whether they have been accepted in the new environment after the war. This has been discussed in American psychiatry journals and so on. Once the person comes back from war, it is very debatable whether he or she will be able to adapt himself to the new environment. Such suicidal attempts are not surprising; however, they are not decisive as to a specific diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your diagnosis of Mr. Landzo of a personality disorder with PTSD, is it an abnormality of the mind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I can say that this is an abnormality of the mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What definition do you have in mind when asking this question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I don't have any definition that I've put forward to him, except the memorandum of law that I faxed to him in Zagreb, Your Honour. Based upon the definitions that I've given him before, would it rise to the level of an abnormality of mind? I sent him the memorandum of law that I did on the Homicide Act of 1957 from the UK

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Because of your forensic experience and the definitions that have been provided to you, does your diagnosis rise to the level of an abnormality of mind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I must give you some additional explanation, because this is related to the issue of the defining of illness/disease and the personality disorders and the difference between those two concepts. When I spoke about what is a disease and what is not a disease, I was using criteria that have been generally accepted in Europe, and I have compared them with our tradition. According to the European psychiatry, this would not fall into the category of disease, but this doesn't mean that some other system, like an American system, would not classify a PTSD as a disease. However, when we talk about personality disorders, anxieties, the PTSD would fall under the category of anxiety. We are dealing with mental states which are borderline cases between health and mental disease. I was comparing this with something that can be termed as an abnormality of the mind for sure, but this is not a pathology of the personality. What you have given to me is actually a legal definition of the abnormality of the mind, and this is my position on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Goreta, after your review of the evidence and seeing Esad Landzo today, in October of 1998, do you consider that he would be any threat to society if released today?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I cannot claim that with certainty. This should be decided by the persons who are in charge of his treatment and who will be evaluating all aspects of his behaviour. Of course, another criteria would be his actual behaviour once he is released from custody. But what I can say now, and in view of what I have examined, I can say that there have been significant, positive changes with the accused. One cannot see that there is any type of aggressive orientation of the accused towards the environment. However, there is a so-called counterphobic manoeuvring, and this, I believe, has been stated in some other expert opinions. This has to be viewed in relation to his overidentifying himself with the legal system itself and his emphasised need to start anew. He, himself, has used terms such as "building up of a new personality," and so on. This is probably something that he has come across during his therapy. However, on the basis of the documentation that has been provided to me, and on the basis of my conversation with the accused, I can clearly see a wish, a need, to fully adapt himself to the environment. In as much as he wanted to be a perfect soldier during the war, he now is trying to be a perfect detainee, and he is also trying to be a perfect patient. We can, therefore, think that he will want to be a perfect rehabilitated person. I may be over-optimistic, and this may not conform with the reality; however, on the basis of what I have learned in my conversations with him, the fact is that he has made significant progression during his therapy. Again, provided that all the criteria, all the requirements which I have mentioned are met, I think that he has a fairly good prognosis in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I pass the witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you any other witnesses to call?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have another witness to call, but I believe the Prosecutor would love to have some cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The other accused, do they have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution does have cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do any of you have cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, the Defence of Zejnil Delalic has no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Mucic has a number of issues to raise with this witness, and I will be as brief as I possibly can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Goreta, you have said in your evidence this afternoon, as far as Mr. Landzo is concerned, that some of his problems relate to incidents and causation in his childhood; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes. I did understand that his problems from childhood were mentioned, but not specifically. However, I may be able to start my answer, and then the additional questions may be asked. As far as his childhood is concerned, and I did not have an opportunity to come to a full reconstruction of it, I only know it from the materials that I have read, what may be needed to be taken into consideration was the asthmatic bronchitis which he suffered from; however, I did not see the relevant documents in that regard. There were frequent visits and stays in the hospital. Such early separations from the family, primarily from his mother, may be a relevant and significant cause for a future disorder. The asthma itself, this asthmatic bronchitis, is a psychosomatic condition which often entails psychological problems which relates to dependency, need for protection, need for security, and the need to rely on others. When such needs are not satisfied or frustrated early on, it all may have significant consequences. In the documents I have read, his isolation is also discussed, which, at that time, was compensated through association with dogs, stray dogs, which, to him, were compensation for his inadequate relations with his peers. This could be one of the reasons for his withdrawal, his insecurity, his avoiding people. Again, another reason that has been mentioned frequently is that he could not participate in physical activities at the same level with others because he had problems with breathing. Allegedly, other kids were mocking him, and he was an object of jokes. These are, sort of, relatively banal incidents from his everyday life, but it could have been fateful for his development, especially if they occurred so early in his childhood. This is what I had in mind when I referred to his childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I hadn't realised I'd asked such a long question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: What I really wanted to establish is that if there were any psychological trauma in his childhood, it's plain, is it not, that that predates any causation arising out of the incidents to which this trial relates? That must be right, mustn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I could answer this question in detail had I conducted a full expert analysis, such as an expert's approach should be. However, my mission here was much more limited. In compliance with that, I can just provide you this aspect of his childhood, but I cannot speak fully to those issues in a way that would be satisfactory to me and to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think there was some witness produced by you who said that he used to play football, even though as a goalkeeper, with the other school boys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I don't think I produced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think Ms. McMurrey, one of her other witnesses talked about his playing football with the other boys, even though as a goalkeeper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's an observation and a line of questioning, Your Honour, into which, you'll be pleased to know, I'm not going to draw this witness, on the basis that the psychological analysis of football is likely to take us at least a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I was saying group games. If you were withdrawn, you wouldn't be taking part in group games, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I wouldn't, that's for sure, Your Honour. I'm afraid that my footballing years are long past.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Let me try and ask you some questions to which the answers may be "yes" or "no." You based your analysis of Mr. Landzo, essentially, from reading the reports of others and a three-and-a-half-hour interview that you conducted yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes. I said that, and that is correct. These are actually the boundaries of confidence or certainty in which I can address these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: One important predicate is that Mr. Landzo, when giving information to others or to yourself, is telling the truth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: The question of truth was also raised with the psychiatrists which were involved in this matter. We do not assess the truthfulness, unless we are requested to directly testify to the veracity of a certain witness's testimony, but even then, our conclusions are not simply "yes" or "no," but just to provide psychiatric elements to the degree of potential veracity based on the psychological factors which may contribute to reaching conclusions as to the veracity of a particular witness. Now, as to the veracity of Mr. Landzo himself, I don't think that I can, and I don't think that I should, offer my views here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: With respect, Dr. Goreta, I'm not asking you for your views as to whether or not he was telling the truth. That's a matter for the learned Judges. They determine whether or not they believe a matter is true or not true in the context of the trial. What I'm putting to you is this: If you are asking anybody, Mr. Landzo or anybody else, for that matter, questions, your analysis, based upon his answers, is going to be affected by whether or not he is telling the truth in answer to those questions. That must be correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: If any inference is to be drawn, and I'm now speaking purely on behalf of Mr. Mucic, if any inference is to be drawn adverse to Mr. Mucic, in considering the element of mitigation in this sentence, out of what Mr. Landzo has said, either to you or to anybody else, his credibility, his veracity, is central to the issue, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: So if, during the course of the case, there was anything that would cast doubt upon that veracity, that would be a significant feature; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: That would be significant. However, if you will allow me to elaborate on this, rather than answer with "yes" or "no," when an expert has communication with the person he is questioning, he does not proceed in a vacuum, and he has to consider the acts in a case file which have been described as criminal acts. That has to be taken into account, and that will constitute one of the elements. He will also make an assumption that the interviewee is actually speaking the truth. If, later on, it turns out that either of the versions which were received, either from the documents or through the interviewee, if they are not true, or any other facts came to light which would bring into question any of this, then the psychiatrist, himself, is free to change his opinion and to take into account those subsequent circumstances or facts which contribute to his overall opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to be so bold as to assume that you've understood the line of questioning that I undertook in this case and the purpose of it. If that point has been made, that's all I sought to do. Thank you very much. Thank you, Dr. Goreta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: One thing, Judge. I just have to get wired up here. I believe we're wired up now. May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Hi, Doctor. My name is Tom Moran. Let me reintroduce myself. I think we met a couple of times in the Defence room, just in passing. I'm going to ask you a few questions, and some of them will require "yes" or "no," but the first one you may want to explain something. You are, of course, an expert in post-traumatic stress syndrome. You have a special expertise in that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: No. I do not define myself as a PTSD expert. I was called here by other persons who thought that I could say certain things about that. I'm not an expert in such a narrow area. I cover a much wider scope of issues in forensic science.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In your experience, have you testified or provided evidence in criminal cases, both before and after the war, as it applies to mitigation of punishment? That may not have been a very artfully-phrased question. If you don't understand it, I would be happy to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: A large part of our expertise is trying to determine the level of mental responsibility, and that is what often determines the punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: This may be outside your expertise, and if it is, that's fine, but do you know how the courts in the former Yugoslavia treated post-traumatic stress syndrome as it related to mitigation of punishment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: The courts in the former Yugoslavia, for the most part, did not deal with PTSD, because it became very topical during and after the war. I do not recall that, in that period, I personally was ever called to provide expert opinion on such cases, but after the war, unfortunately, this was very frequently the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do the courts in Yugoslavia consider mental, and I'll use the phrase "disorders," which may not be the correct phrase, but mental disorders such as post-traumatic stress syndrome, to be mitigating in punishment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: The courts in Yugoslavia do not connect any kind of mental responsibility with any kind of act. They always seek the experts to define, as closely as possible, the state of mental health of a person at the time of the crime. That is basically what they have us define for them. If the Court accepts the expert opinion of a psychiatrist, then such person is not considered criminally responsible. It is quite probable that in cases such as psychosis and schizophrenia, 70 to 80 per cent of the cases will result in such a conclusion that such a person was not criminally responsible, but that does not mean that it will be the case in 100 per cent of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What I was getting at was not just completely relieving someone from criminal responsibility, but, rather, reducing the punishment based upon some kind of mental disease or mental defect and whether, although they would still be criminally responsible, the courts took that into consideration in assessing punishment. They did? Okay. Doctor, let me go on to something else. I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes. The Court always allowed the possibility that any diagnosis would be linked to the mitigation of sentence, but they needed to be provided with a reliable opinion. Frequently, a diagnosis would not necessarily result in any mitigation of sentence, because this person may have had a certain mental disorder at the time but still would be responsible enough and knew well enough what his acts were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's fine, Doctor. Let me go on to something else. You talked about this HOS camp where Mr. Landzo supposedly was taught how to murder people. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, what is HOS, H-O-S, what is this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: HOS is an abbreviation. I'm not sure if I will be able to say it correctly, but it seems like Croatian liberation forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's close enough for government work.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: But I am afraid that this would not be a question for a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's fine. Let me go on to something that would be a question for a psychiatrist, though. You, of course, have treated a lot of people who have been engaged in activities during the war, the whole period of the war from early until late; is that correct, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You and your colleagues have probably seen a very, very broad spectrum of people who were engaged in the fighting and saw horrible things during the war and came to you later for psychiatric help?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, has any of your other patients told you that they were around some kind of a HOS camp, especially early in the war, where people were brought in and prisoners were murdered in front of these people so that they could learn how to kill? Have you ever heard -- have any of your other patients ever told you anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I, personally, have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of any of your other patients tell you that they were around some kind of camp where murders were occurring, and after they were there for awhile and had seen a bunch of murders, the people in charge of the camp said, "If you want to leave, just go ahead and go"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: No. I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Of course, you're --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: But perhaps, if I may just add, apart from working in forensic psychiatry in a position in which I've been in the last four or five years, I'm a clinical physician, and I have conducted therapy of a number of patients with PTSD, some of whom were individuals who spent some time in camps and who related similar types of experiences. There are a number of issues regarding the organisation of camps, but I do not have pertinent documents in that regard, and you may be better advised to look elsewhere for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. I'm sure that Mr. Niemann has in his files a lot of information about that kind of thing. Let me go on to a different subject, Doctor, if I could. There is a diagnosis that we use in America in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual called anti-social personality disorder. You're familiar with that diagnosis, aren't you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It used to be called sociopathy, didn't it, in the DSM-II?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: It's one of the synonyms I mentioned earlier. There's a whole spectrum, gamut of synonyms, some of which have been completely abandoned, precisely, because of the negative connotations, and sociopathy is something that has been abandoned for those reasons precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When talking about anti-personality disorder, anti-social personality disorder, sociopathy, are some of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm going to object to Mr. Moran. The Doctor has said that that's been abandoned. That's not a term used today and he continues to say that all are sociopathy, and it is abandoned for the reasons that Mr. Moran is using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In any case, Mr. Moran, how does it help you with the plea of mitigation taken up by Landzo as being accepted, or not accepted, or partly accepted? How will that interest you? It will be taken into account only if we find Mr. Landzo guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand that. What I'm worried about is that there's been some documents presented by Mr. Landzo's lawyers which purport to being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It will only be seen once we've decided if Mr. Landzo is guilty or not, and how would that affect your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, certain of those documents could affect my client very greatly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If his plea is accepted, then your client would get a more serious sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. Let me go over my notes, and then I think I'll be done, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Is it common, Doctor, for persons suffering from anti-social personality disorder to do things like shift blame for their bad acts to others?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We already have evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. Then I will just pass the witness Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If you think that only the experts have said that they shift blame onto each others, but also that they are frequently good liars. This is what the psychiatrists have said before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When you start asking questions, I get surprised, because much of the evidence you have is already on the record. So I don't know what you're arguing about. Are there any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, I'm Teresa McHenry?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution. I would like to go through this quickly, and I want to be fair to you. I'm going to ask you a number of questions, some of which I hope only require a "yes" or a "no" or "I don't know." If I ask you, in effect, a "yes" or "no" or "I don't know" question, and you don't believe you can fairly answer it with a "yes" or "no" or "I don't know," please just tell me that before you start explaining your answer, because for some of the questions, I may just go on to another question rather than take up the time necessary that you believe to explore the matter fully, okay? Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Also, to make sure I'm fair to you, sir, I have some questions about your report, and let me just ask you: Did you write this report yourself in English?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: No. The report was translated into English. My English is not good enough for me to dare make a translation for court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: If I may clarify, my English is good enough that I can control whether the translation is an authentic translation of my Croatian original.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you indicated that you went through some expert reports and some transcript of proceedings from, you believe, July of this year. Am I correct that you did not review the testimony of any of the victims of Mr. Landzo's crimes concerning his behaviour in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I reviewed only what I have said I did and what I have received from the Defence counsel, which was, I think, in October. She can probably tell you exactly what was contained in there, but I think it was only the experts' reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to ask that Ms. McHenry refrain from making it a statement of the crimes he's committed. He has not been found guilty of these crimes yet, and she's assuming he's been found guilty, and she's misleading the witness by saying so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think she was probably asking whether he had met any of the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, the testimony of the victims. That's what I heard her ask, whether she went through the testimony of the victims. I think that's a normal thing if one wants to go through the whole exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, my submission is they are alleged victims at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They are victims. In ordinary English language, they are victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have admitted some of the charges partly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, did you review the expert report of the psychiatrist from Bosnia-Herzegovina, a report from 1992 about events -- I'm sorry, a report from 1994 about events in 1992 which found that Mr. Landzo did not have significant diminished mental responsibility? Were you given access to that report, sir, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I read all expert reports which were contained in the file. If I recall correctly, there was an expert report by Dr. -- and maybe you can remind me of the name, who, if I remember correctly, opined that Mr. Landzo, in a case in which he offered his expertise, his intellectual capacities were fully intact, and I think that they were somewhat diminished, but not significantly diminished. I don't know if that's the expertise that you're referring to. I must, again, remind you that I have read large quantities of materials, and I cannot, at all times, give you very specific information, but I could comment on it again if I were given it to review again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, your report indicates that what you are giving is a preliminary opinion. Can you explain what you mean by "preliminary opinion"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: A preliminary opinion is a short report on the basis of all the documents which I reviewed so far and on the basis of the conversation I had. In other words, with the reservation that I did not conduct a full expert report. Also, if any new facts would come to light which would bring into question my conclusions, then, obviously, and I stated this today, certain corrections would be possible, in other words, a preliminary opinion is a very short report, and it is not the way I usually write my expert opinions. But I was given to believe that this Court would accept this form. In any event, this is the first time that I'm testifying as an expert report for one of the parties here. This is not the practice we have in my home jurisdiction where we are usually called by the Courts to provide opinions to both parties, all parties concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just ask Ms. McHenry to direct us to what paragraph she sees the word "preliminary"?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Second paragraph on page 2, where he says: "I can give the following preliminary opinion." If that helps you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, going forward, I understood you to say that Mr. Landzo had some significant personality problems at the present time and that he had those in 1992. I take it you would agree that Mr. Landzo still has, in your view, at least, a dependent personality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you would agree, sir, that if Mr. Landzo was to return to Bosnia-Herzegovina for any reason, such as that no other country wished to accept him, there could be some problems; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes. I've also explained that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Even if he did go to another country, if he wasn't extremely closely supervised and if his role model was a not-positive person, you would agree that there would be some serious problems then too; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Can I say more than "yes" or "no" in response to that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it the case that you don't think you can fairly answer that question with a "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I don't think I can. I've already explained certain things as to these criteria and preconditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose counsel is basing the next question on your theory that you still believe that Landzo has a dependent personality. This is the basis on which her question was put.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I believe that I have given answers to all these questions, but if necessary, if I'm requested to do so, I can give further explanation as to the circumstances in which he may find himself one day, both positive and negative, circumstances that would propose a risk in any other country.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me just move forward, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the witness should be allowed to answer the question. He said he was not able to answer it fully, and he would like to explain. I believe if she is going to ask the question and he says that he needs to explain, that he should be allowed to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you pursuing the question or are you still wanting to ask some other question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm not pursuing it. I'm making the decision that in terms of going quickly, that he has sufficiently explained it enough in his direct. Of course, Ms. McMurrey can ask, with Your Honours' permission, what she believes appropriate re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Carry on with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you were asked some hypothetical questions by Ms. McMurrey about the behaviour of normal, intelligent people during the war. Is it your opinion that Mr. Landzo was a normal person before and during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo, with the personality disorder that he has, he must have had such symptoms as early as childhood. As I have already stated today, the continuation of these symptoms is always connected to early childhood, and any diagnosis, according to the classifications that I mentioned, can be only made after the age of 18, because this falls within the category of personality disorder of adult persons. These disorders can be diagnosed early on, but bearing in mind certain other categories, certain other disorders, this can be changed later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it correct then, sir, that you would agree with me that, according to your opinion, prior to the war, Mr. Landzo was not a normal person?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I will agree with you that, at that time, he must have had certain basic symptoms of personality disorders which, later on, were manifested as symptoms of dependent personality disorder. In certain circumstances, these symptoms can go unnoticed, and this type of behaviour can never be termed as psychopathological type of behaviour. However, in certain adverse conditions, this may lead to this kind of behaviour. People who suffer from personality disorders are not necessarily people who are not very well adapted to the society. However, in certain circumstances, such as the war, these personality disorders can be emphasised, can be reinforced and worsened. In some other circumstances, such individuals would have never exhibited symptoms of personality disorders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I take it, from your testimony, that although you would opine that Mr. Landzo is not suffering from PTSD at the present time, you would disagree with any contention that he has recovered completely from any mental difficulties or personality difficulties he may have had in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I cannot claim that. This is something that I have already stated and written in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you're aware that one Defence expert witness, Dr. Gripon, who interviewed Mr. Landzo for some 40 hours and interviewed a number of his friends and relatives, testified that Mr. Landzo had committed anti-social and violent behaviour before he was a guard in Celebici and after he was a guard in Celebici. Do you agree or disagree with that statement, or do you not have enough information to give an opinion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I believe I have already answered that question in response to the question regarding differences in opinion of various psychiatrists. Certain aggressive types of behaviour, by themselves, cannot always be sufficient for a diagnosis of a personality disorder -- dissocial personality disorder. This dissocial personality disorder is defined as a continuous tendency towards criminal behaviour. So, in respect of that part of the report of Dr. Gripon, I cannot agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you agree that avoidance is a fundamental characteristic of anyone suffering from PTSD?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Avoidance is one of the categories that is a criterion for the diagnosis of PTSD. According to this criteria, it should be present. However, to the extent I have reviewed the relevant documentation, and this is going back to a discussion we've already had, is that this type of avoidance cannot be a criterion for this particular diagnosis. There is a whole range of defensive mechanisms that are involved here, one of them being, the person reacted in quite an opposite way. It is confronted with the cause of his or her fear in order for the fear to be avoided. We cannot adopt a reductionist attitude here, in view of the number of criteria. We should simply count the points that any criteria is worth, and on the basis of that, we can provide a psychiatric diagnosis. In addition to the clinical picture of the patient at a particular moment, we have to bear in mind the development of the PTSD, because there can be periods where there are no symptoms at all; however, the person is still suffering from the PTSD and in a very acute way. These symptoms can be hyperthymic at one particular point. However, this has to be viewed within the context of the whole situation, even when providing a diagnosis for the PTSD.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, during your direct testimony, you indicated that Mr. Landzo was very cooperative, except for a few areas which he justified based on a lack of memory. Did the lack of memory that Mr. Landzo told you about, did that have to do with the alleged crimes committed in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Partly to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that among the personality difficulties in PTSD that you believe Mr. Landzo has, lack of memory is not a normal characteristic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Lack of memory is one of the symptoms of the PTSD; however, it's not very characteristic. The diagnosis of the PTSD can be offered, regardless of the lack of memory, with it or without it. Lack of memory is not a psychiatric diagnosis. It's a symptom that can be found in a various number of psychiatric diagnoses. Its causes can be various. It can range from these that have been mentioned in these proceedings, that is, a conscious, intentional correcting of the statement for the purpose of protecting one's position in the criminal proceedings to some unconscious phenomena which can be found with normal people as well. Certain people cannot simply confront themselves with their past behaviour and may experience a complete amnesia as to certain events. This can be caused by some physical causes, such as contusions and so on. I don't think it is necessary to go further into this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you would agree with me that during your interview with Mr. Landzo, you noted that he had certain difficulties with control over his emotional reactions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The prior experts, both Prosecution and Defence experts, uniformly talked about a pronounced lack of empathy and lack of remorse in Mr. Landzo. Is that consistent or inconsistent with your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Lack of remorse in his case, at least as far as verbal expression of it is concerned, I do not think exists. He mentioned to me on several occasions that he feels guilty and that he feels the need to be punished. If that need is not satisfied, he doesn't believe that he could find his balance once again, that he would be able to live normally again. The problem of guilt, at a deeper level, is another problem, and this was the central issue in my doctoral thesis. I just want to say that in his communication with me, Mr. Landzo did express messages in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Landzo has a narcissistic pathology. What do you mean by narcissistic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I believe that that question has been answered as well. To put it in simple terms, the narcissistic pathology concerns the difficulty of assessing one's own worth, and it goes to the issue of self-respect and the respect that comes from others as well. Such a person has a permanent need to test his or her environment, and he needs to be recognised all the time. He has to receive this type of stimuli all the time. We have also had cases in which such persons wanted to show him or herself in a much better light and present himself as a better person than others. In order to avoid any misunderstanding --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you agree that narcissistic also, usually, means in a very strong --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. Ms. McHenry didn't let Dr. Goreta finish his answer. He was in mid-sentence when she interrupted him. I ask that she just, please, allow him to finish his answer to the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If I interrupted the witness, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Thank you. I only wanted to add one more sentence, because there may have been a certain misunderstanding in relation to this issue. Laypersons tend to label, as narcissistic persons, those who enjoy public appearance and they tend to believe that persons who are shy are not narcissistic. These are two aspects of one in the same problem. These are only two different manifestations of one in the same problem. A person who is very shy, keeps to himself, does not mean that he is not necessarily narcissistic. Such a person can also act as a public person, but we have to take into account his external behaviour and relevant circumstances. This picture can change in a very short period of time, and this is also the case with narcissistic persons. If such a person should lose respect within his environment, he's even prepared to attempt suicide, and this is another example of what I said earlier on, that suicidal attempts can be symptoms of various types of disorders. There are many examples of that. You probably know of cases of very famous persons who attempted or committed suicide at the moment when their worth and importance was brought into question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked a question about sadistic behaviour, and let me ask you about that: Hypothetically, if you have a person who commits violent acts intended to cause pain, including, setting people on fire or putting lit fuses in their anuses, and if that person reports that he enjoyed mistreating people and if that person reports that one of the reasons he mistreated people was because he was bored and frustrated, in your opinion, is that person exhibiting sadistic behaviour?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: What you have just described are elements of sadistic behaviour. However, they should be put in the context of the overall situation which leads the individual to behave that way. If that person is, on his own, looking for such situations, searching for these type of incidents ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to really move along quickly. If you don't feel you can answer a question with a "yes" or "no," please tell me in the beginning and I may choose to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm going to object again. He was just explaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: These are simple English words. You do not need a psychiatrist or anybody to tell you who is sadistic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The doctor would like to put it in the context of what he's trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you are satisfied, if you are not, then you pass on to whatever issue --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I haven't yet said the key sentence as to the definition of sadism. It's not only physical torture. The basic definition of sadism is the need to have power over another person, to have absolute power and to keep that person under control and in some kind of suspense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: But enjoying it, a person who enjoys pain who --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, enjoying it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated in your examination of war crimes committed in Croatia, you found alcohol or drug abuse in a number of them; is that correct? Just a "yes" or "no" would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: A significant number of them, because, again, I don't have an opportunity to say that there are actually three categories. The number would range from 30 per cent and more of persons who experienced problems with alcohol, but that doesn't mean that they were addicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that there is evidence that Mr. Landzo abused alcohol or drugs in 1992, although he may not have been an addict? Were you aware of that information, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, in your opinion, can the use of drugs or alcohol be a basis of diminished responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: It can be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, you also talked about a phenomena you described that included suspicious Serbs and related topics. Are you suggesting that when a person commits a crime against a person of another ethnic group, because he views all persons from that ethnic group as the enemy, in your view, is that a basis of diminished responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
