utterances.text: No, no, but, again, I'm afraid I cannot give you a "yes" or "no" answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: With your permission, I would like to explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I just want today clarify. You're not suggesting that with suspicious Serbs or with persons who have superegos, or with persons that have transferred aggression, you're not suggesting that the existence of those phenomena is, itself, a basis for diminished responsibility, are you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: If you will allow me, because I cannot simply yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You can explain your answers.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I do not wish, because this was a war between Croats, Muslims, Serbs, I do not wish to take any explanation which mentions a particular nationality. I don't want it to be taken as a basis for diminished responsibility. These were specific problems. But if there is a paranoid experience of other people, if other persons are viewed as people who will harm us in some way, and in that particular situation, those people were Serbs. This is not a psychiatric problem, but the psychiatric problem can take place because of the overall situation. If I see a person who is a Serb, and because of my paranoid state, I connect these persons with all other events, then this can, indeed, be a basis for diminished responsibility, because of that paranoid view of that person, not because of his or her ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me just turn now, sir, to the study that you did in 1994, and it's been introduced. You studied 25 soldiers and gave your expert opinion. Can you tell us, were you just trying to understand or explain their conduct or were you trying to excuse or mitigate their conduct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Again, I cannot say "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please explain, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I think that one of the aspects of the role of the psychiatrist is not to be someone who will be passing moral judgements. The role of the psychiatrist is to offer certain psychological expertise so that a certain category can be viewed as normal or abnormal and so on. In view of that, how can a particular person be assessed? So psychiatrists should offer to the Court their evaluation of a particular behaviour at the relevant times and say whether this could be taken as a foundation, as a basis, for diminished responsibility. It is the discretion of the Court to evaluate diminished responsibility. We provide an explanation, but we do not provide justification for criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, of the 25 soldiers that you examined and gave your expert opinion, and I'm referring to pages 512 to 513 of your article, it's correct that of 12 of those or almost half you found essentially diminished responsibility, and in the other 13, you also found diminished responsibility, such that it would be regarded as a mitigating circumstance; is that correct, sir, that in every case, you either found diminished responsibility such that it could be a mitigating circumstance, or essentially diminished responsibility which is even stronger?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: These data are correct. However, I should add something: This is a selected material, this is a choice or selection of material, because in our centre, we have been receiving the most complex and the most serious cases from the republic. So this can be misleading from the statistical point of view, because many of these individuals who were evaluated somewhere else did not get such harsh, such a severe evaluation. As part of the evaluation of severely diminished responsibility, as far as severely diminished responsibility is concerned, this was only considered as a mitigating circumstance, and the evaluation of that often led to the mitigation of punishment. Where there were cases of capital punishment, the capital punishment was often remitted. I just wanted to say that the courts were not bound to incorporate our evaluation in the verdict.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have four questions, if I might.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Goreta, based on the questioning by counsel for Mucic, his main thrust of his questions was when you listened to the individual, you have to see whether they are telling the truth, but the truth is, as a forensic expert, you look at the total picture, you look at their behaviour, and you look at the materials that you've read, and because you're an expert, you're able to look for signs of malingering?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is this supposed to be a question? What are you trying to accomplish or ratify.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm asking if this is what he looks for, the total picture, or one dimension of whether the person is telling the truth or not. There are more variables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Are there more variables that you look for when interviewing an individual rather than whether they are telling the truth or not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Again, let me repeat, as an expert or as a person who has experience in recognising these reactions, including the false representation, I am able to discern that, but I will not say in court that this person was lying and that he did or did not do whatever he is alleged in these proceedings of the trial that is conducted. We have to offer to the Court, indicia, that is, we have to point to the lack of veracity, if you will, and the conclusions are always those that will be drawn by the Court. If I may just add, it is known that certain disorders such as, histrionic disorder, that people will often present themselves in a false light so that they would present themselves in a false light, let's say, of success. This is something that we also mentioned in connection with narcissism, so there is a tendency for this person to lie, but we have to be reserved about expressing our views on whether such a person is, actually, lying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you, as an expert, are trained to be able to see through that and look at other variables, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: Again, we always, we always look for all the characteristics that would provide the full picture of the mental state of our subject, both during our interview and at the time of the commission of the crime. I have to point out that today in Croatia, defendants often use silence as a defence. This is something that is very widespread. So what we have to do is look for all kinds of additional information which can be described as collateral information, anything that we can find up to the point when we're called to provide our opinion. In some cases, this is not frequently so, but occasionally, if we receive significantly different information, let's say, with respect to a person who offered a defence by silence, and at some point this person has actually decided to talk, then we are brought in to provide an additional or widened opinion on whether they told the truth or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will rise and reassemble at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just raise a matter very quickly? Just after 5.00, might I be excused? Ms. McHenry will take over this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You may be excused. You may continue, Ms. McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Dr. Goreta, no matter how much the counsel for Delic talked about this anti-social personality disorder, that is not Esad Landzo, is it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: I believe I have already answered that question in detail. If you need any further explanations, then I think I would need very specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Although Ms. McHenry did not let you finish one of your answers a while ago, Ms. McHenry asked you about sadistic behaviour. Now, there are other explanations for people exhibiting something that may look like sadistic behaviour. Can you explain what you wanted to tell the Court earlier?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: The second model, which may have some external aspects of sadistic behaviour, is conditioned by a combination of these dependent personality disorder characteristics. I explained the identification, the need to identify with the superior, this afternoon, and this relates to the person who fully trusts his superior and upon whom the subject projects complete responsibility for his behaviour. So if this is the model, according to which one can have sadistic -- if this model is taken into view, then we cannot talk about a sadistic type of personality. The sadistic type of personality is the problem of persons who exhibit other types of criminal behaviour. This kind of person, very often, cannot offer any resistance or does not wish to offer any resistance to the person issuing orders, because that individual believes that the superior knows better than he does and that the superior would take upon himself the responsibility for his acts. Here, I'm talking about a certain model of behaviour without giving any specific examples and involving any persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, the last question is that Ms. McHenry had asked you, "If Mr. Landzo goes to another country and he has a bad role model, would it turn out with the same results that it has before?" Can you explain why it would be different now than it was before?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm going to object. I don't think this arises out of re-examination and, certainly, that was not my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It was put not exactly the same way. I think what Ms. McHenry was suggesting is, if he was somewhere else, whether he would manifest the same traits. That is not putting it as you have put it, whether he had another role model, which is quite a different thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then I will phrase it according to what the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not what the Court wishes, what you wish and what the cross-examination inferred, not what the Court wishes. It's not the Court's question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you, Doctor, is what would be the difference in his behaviour today compared to 1992, if he's moved into a situation where, let's say, he might be exposed to a Mafia Don in Chicago. What would be the difference?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV GORETA
utterances.text: For everybody, including persons who are at risk because of the changed structure of personality, it wouldn't be very healthy or advisable to be in a Mafia environment. I think this is common knowledge. You don't need a psychiatrist to offer any explanation in that respect. What can be expected is that, whatever the fate of Mr. Landzo is, he will be treated in accordance with all known penological principles and models. This was purely a hypothetical situation. I wanted to say that he certainly needs certain psychotherapy in prison and that the continuation of such psychotherapy should be ensured. Once he leaves the prison environment, as I said, he will have to spend a certain period of time, and that is to be assessed only later on, I mean, the length of that period. So he will have to be under the supervision of certain experts until it is fully established and evaluated that Mr. Landzo is in full control, like any other citizen, of his moral responsibility. This is something that cannot be very precisely defined at this particular moment. However, on the basis of my knowledge and the conversations I had, I can say that this is all moving towards a positive outcome. I think that Mr. Landzo has a chance to improve in that regard. Whether this particular process will stop because of inappropriate care and inadequate experts, this is something else. I have mentioned, I believe, the factors that are decisive for the idea that I have just exposed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: As compared between 1992 and 1998, has Mr. Landzo matured?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. This does not rise out of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Has he developed better coping skills?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that different from your last question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think it's different because he's able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it did not arise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then I certainly thank you for coming here on your birthday, Dr. Goreta, and I appreciate the testimony you have offered for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. You have been very helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would also like to thank this Honourable Chamber for listening to me, and it has been a privilege and an honour for me to participate in the proceedings. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are discharged. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have your next witness now?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Defence of Esad Landzo calls Goran Jelisic. Your Honours, just for completeness of the written statements, I was just handed something that I did not file, the original written statement by one of my witnesses with the original signature, so I would like to offer that now. The copies were already filed earlier. If I might, I'll wait for the assistance of the usher. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jelisic. You and I met for the first time Friday afternoon, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: My name is Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You're currently charged under indictment in this Tribunal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background, Mr. Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: I'm orthodox by religion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Are you currently residing at the U.N. detention unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: What date did you arrive there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of January, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Do you know a young man named Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court your first encounter with Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Would you do it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: I arrived in the detention unit of the United Nations, as I've already said, on the 22nd of January, 1998. On the 23rd of January at 1.00 p.m., I was allowed contact with other detainees. The guards came at around 1.00, opened the doors of my cell, and then left. I heard voices from other rooms, but I couldn't tell where they were coming from. I simply stood at the door. I didn't know where to go. At that moment, I was approached by Esad Landzo and another detainee of the U.N. detention unit. They were walking through the corridor, and Esad Landzo, I remember very well, said, "Come on here, you brother Serb. Don't fear anything." Then he and the other detainee took me to our living room, and they introduced me to other detainees. After that, Esad Landzo took me to his cell, and he showed me around. He showed me his computer. He told me what he was doing, and we spent some time talking. That was our first encounter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Since that time, have you spent a lot of time with Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did he try to explain the proceedings to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was Esad Landzo who explained to me that I would have an initial appearance a few days later on. He explained to me how this functioned, what the procedure was, and he told me that we were all together there and that we could normally socialise with each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you first arrived there, did he also provide you with some clothing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. For my initial appearance before the International Tribunal, which took place four days later, Esad Landzo gave me a shirt, a tie, and a blazer. Other detainees lent me their shoes and some other items of clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Does he assist the people in the detention centre with translation or interpretation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes, he does. Together with another group of us detainees in the Dutch section of the prison, Esad Landzo is assisting us with the translation/interpretation in the absence of our interpreter. He helps us with the computer, and he is also a very good cook. He's been preparing meals for us on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you and Mr. Landzo together initiate special joint celebrations for religious holidays at the detention centre?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Upon my arrival at the detention unit, the first religious holiday was a Muslim holiday, the Bajram. On that occasion, I helped Esad Landzo organise the celebration, so we celebrated it together. After that, I helped him clean the place and tidy up the premises. When the orthodox religious holiday came, Esad Landzo helped me and other detainees of orthodox religion with the arranging of the celebration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Were you even subjected to criticism by some of the other Serb detainees for your association with Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That was mainly only one other detainee, though, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, does Esad Landzo like children too?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes, he does. Whenever I had a visit from my wife and my 3-year-old son, Esad Landzo would prepare food for my family, and he would take care of my son. He would play ball with him and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you have telephone conversations, does he send messages back to your family?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes, he does. It can be seen from the conversations at the detention unit, which are taped, whenever I talk to my family, they send their regards to Esad Landzo, and Esad Landzo always sends regards to my family, my wife and other members of my family.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you first arrived here, trying to face the serious accusations that you're charged with, was there a time when Esad Landzo helped you deal with these things?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In what way did he help you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: He helped me by explaining to me how things worked. He gave me some advice and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Judge McDonald came to visit all of you at the U.N. detention centre too, didn't she?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Was Judge McDonald impressed with the camaraderie that she saw between all of you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: What did she tell you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: The last time Judge McDonald was there, they held a meeting which lasted about three hours. We discussed all our problems. One discussion centred around the fact that, through this Tribunal, a lasting peace needs to be established in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later on when we sat together, we said that we found peace among ourselves, but how those over there are going to reach it was another matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jelisic, do you know the other Celebici defendants back here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Have you ever had any problems with them whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Are you aware of Esad Landzo's problems with bronchitis or asthma?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: He told me a little bit about his health problems, but as I often spend some time in his cell, I saw that he had two small pumps for his asthma.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Does his asthma seem to be better since he has regular medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: When you first met Esad Landzo, was he going through certain periods of depression?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: I saw that he was taking a lot of pills. Several months ago, I don't know exactly when, for about five or six days, he did not leave his cell, and I became concerned because we are good friends. So I went over there, and he asked me to leave the room. I could tell that he was going through some major problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Could you tell a big difference in Esad Landzo after he came before the Tribunal and testified?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Esad Landzo does not use anything anymore as therapy. I asked him several days ago, "Are you taking any pills anymore," and he said, "No, I don't."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did you observe any changes in his personality?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: He just seems more serene. I don't know how to put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In your group over in the Dutch detention centre, you told me how you have all found a bit of humour in each ethnic group. Is there one person in your group that you consider the poet for your group?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber about this poem that you have chosen to express your ideas?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: It's a poem which we put together. In fact, Mr. Zaric wrote it down, and sometimes we actually sing this if we are bored when we're together. This poem, which you have there on paper, is some kind of a message of the U.N. detention unit detainees through which we send a message to our representatives to reach peace for all times, to take into account what we have experienced here, and to take that as a lesson and to achieve a lasting peace. In one of the lines, we also call upon our authorities to cooperate with this institution and to help bring here the real leaders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Does this poem represent the sincere feelings of you and Esad Landzo and your group in the detention centre?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes, the most sincere feelings. We wouldn't have written it down had we not thought so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to introduce this poem into evidence as mitigating evidence, at this point, of rehabilitation and the rehabilitation of the group as a whole in the detention centre. I only have one copy here of the English translation. I don't know if the Court would just allow me to read the last four stanzas, or if you would like to read it yourselves later, I will provide more copies of the English translation. It really is quite moving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's all right. If that's their poem, who translated it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have one translation here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic, this was written in Serb epic poetry style where it all rhymes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The English translation doesn't rhyme, so there may be something lost, but if the Court will allow me, I'll read the last four verses. "It is not important what happened there. It is important how we feel here. Good harmony reigns here among us. Everybody would say it is the way it used to be. They say we are war criminals, and we are just like little kids here. There is fun there. There is the nice gang. No way we are the bad ones. If our compatriots over there only knew how harmoniously we live here, they would lie down on their stomachs and they would destroy their rifles for peace. May this poem be a lesson for all nice and decent people. If there is harmony now in The Hague, follow us. It will be good for everybody."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jelisic, for coming here. Is there anything else you would like to say how Esad Landzo has affected you at the detention centre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have not put in the poem.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The poem, I would like to introduce it into evidence. There are the Bosnian and the English version there.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: If I could just add regarding Esad Landzo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You can say what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another thing that I could add regarding Esad Landzo, which can be seen from the document which about ten of the detainees have signed, that he is a truly social person, very communicative, and a great joker. I also noticed that he really keeps his cell very clean. It is one of the cleanest cells in the unit. He also likes to paint. He now has undertaken to make a painting of my son. He loves sports. We often play football, volleyball, and we socialise. When I came over here to testify regarding the character of Esad Landzo and when I was coming here, all the detainees wished me good luck.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I appreciate you coming today. Thank you. I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence of Mr. Zejnil Delalic has no questions of Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Neither has the Defence of Mr. Mucic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have about three. I think that if I can do it from here, it might quicken the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, my name is Tom Moran, and I represent Hazim Delic. You know Hazim?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm afraid the interpreters couldn't hear Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: My name is Tom Moran, and I represent Hazim Delic. You know Hazim?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, first thing, do you talk to Mr. Delic on a fairly regular basis?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you recall telling him that Mr. Landzo had told you that he was going to come over here and lie about being given orders to commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: On the advice of my lawyer, I do not wish to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I move to strike all of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If he has properly invoked his right against self-incrimination, then I cannot cross-examine him, and his testimony should be stricken from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There are other questions you may ask, not necessarily this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, you are currently in some temporary quarters at the U.N. detention centre, is that correct, not the regular detention centre, but an older area of the prison, you and the rest of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: GORAN JELISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, would it be fair to say that you're confined in an area without toilets, without running water, without a place to wash your hands?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the relevance of this line of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think the relevance is that it shows that the conditions that these people are being held in are not too dissimilar from the conditions in the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I still don't see the relevance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There's no relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Fine. I'll pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No questions from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your helpful testimony. I think you are discharged now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. You can go. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point, of course, the Defence of Esad Landzo has no other oral testimony to put before the Court, but we would like to re-urge that the Court reconsider all mental health testimony in the trial in the light of the purposes for sentencing, because it would be a different test to apply as far as for mitigation of punishment. We have nothing further right now on sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The procedure is an integrated one in which both the arguments for sentencing and for guilt are built into one. So it definitely will be considered together. There's nothing new in that. Any other witnesses you want to call so that we can proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one witness who is in the witness room right now. He is our expert on Yugoslav law. I suspect that the evidence will take about an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has testimony on Yugoslav law and it will take an hour on sentencing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it relates totally to the sentencing in the former Yugoslavia. I have provided the Court with a copy of his report, and he is mainly here to just explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will start with him today, and we will continue with him tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: First, Your Honour, I would submit to the Court, and the Prosecutor has already had these, a series of statements. These are the English translations that were e-mailed to me. We are getting the originals faxed to us of Mr. Delic's father and another relative. His father was unable to come because Mr. Delic's mother is quite ill, and he is just afraid to leave the Konjic area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If it helps expedite matters, the Prosecution has indicated that it does not object to the introduction of this expert witness's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you going to add to the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'd just like to explain any questions that the Court has because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I wish you had given us a copy before so that if there were any doubts, we could clarify them ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was filed last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Don't apologise. Maybe I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There was some confusion over it. In fact, it actually managed to be filed twice. Your Honour, I sometimes think that the document distribution here is almost as bad as the document distribution system in my own office, and sometimes things just do not get around. Let me suggest this, Your Honour: I have one copy of his report here, and I would be more than happy to provide it to you. If you would like, we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe it's lying on my table. I'll check on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Why don't I just provide this one here, the only one that I have and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: His examination-in-chief may not take very long. Just ask him a few questions, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Pardon, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just file your report, and if there are any questions that we want to be answered, we'll ask him. Why have an hour for the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The Prosecution doesn't object to the accuracy of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you think it would expedite things if you took his report, read it overnight, and then we will start with him at 10.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm not sure what difference his explanation will make, because this is a matter of law, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It's also the practice, and the practice might -- for instance, in some jurisdictions, mine, for instance, you see a lot of maximum sentences given. In other jurisdictions, you see lesser sentences given as a practice. Article 24(1) talks about the practice in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That depends on the facts before the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it definitely depends on the facts, but the practice, I think, is what we wanted to bring before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's a very lasting thing. You don't use that because somebody was imposing a certain amount of years. You also would do that merely because he was doing so. It depends on the facts before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It clearly depends on the facts before the Court, and the only other thing that might require some clarification is there is some distinction -- he is taking some dispute with the sentencing judgement in the Tadic case on what Yugoslav law was. He and Judge McDonald disagree about what the law was, and I think that that's something we need to bring before the Court, that it could have been that it wasn't presented as clearly in the Tadic case as it could have been, or whatever, but we wanted to bring that one thing before the Court also. So shall we start with him at 10.00 in the morning, and maybe about 15 minutes in direct, if that much and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This shouldn't take longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour. This is something, if anything, to help you understand. The second thing is we were going to call Mr. Delic's wife. It appears we may not be doing that. We would like permission, if we rest, to submit a written statement from her in the next day or so, if we decide not to call her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we can start tomorrow morning at 10.00 and then carry on. Actually, I've always preferred reading the statute myself, and then I know exactly what the position is, because that's what guides me more than what some other Judges do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I presume we will be done before lunch, well before lunch, just to warn my colleagues that they better have their witnesses here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now rise and resume at 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
